paragraphs.text: From Arius, the foul founder of the impious heresy of the Arians, from his discourse On the Trinity. This, then, is how we must understand the Gospel sayings that say, “I do not seek my own will,” and, “I have come down from heaven not to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me”: the Son's will does not entirely follow and agree with the Father's counsel. That is why he usefully puts the Father's will before his own, saying, “Father, let not my will be done, but yours.” From the same Arius, from the interpretation he wrote against the creed of the Fathers at Nicaea. “For we too,” he says, “were once disobedient, doing the wills of the flesh”; since also

in another place he finds fault with it, saying, “For the mind of the flesh is death, and its will is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be, since it is hostile to God.” So Jesus shared in flesh and blood and took hold of the seed and will of Abraham. Because of this he refuses his own will, saying, “Yet let not my will be done.” And after other things: The divine Scriptures, then, teach us that the Son has one created nature, and from them we also learn about his will, just as also the

From Aetius, the cause of the whole God-fighting Arian heresy, from his discourse On the Son. So the son of Mary does not have two wills. Otherwise the will of God would wage war against a fleshly will, as the laws of the Manichaeans teach. From the same, from the same discourse. For the Son himself explains, in his own person, the substance and the unlikeness of his own nature by refusing to carry out his own will. If, then, the will must be refused, so must the nature. That is why the Son does not disdain to confess the Father as his God and maker, for only the Father's will is good. So the natures of the Son and the Father are different, and their two wills are unlike. From Eunomius, the leading actor on Arius's theatrical [?] stage, from the third discourse On the Son. “For I have come down from heaven,” he says, “not to do my own will, but the will of the Father.” See how the Word who came down from above sets aside his own will because it does not agree with the uncreated will of the Father. This is because the Word has a created nature, and so also a created

From St Eustathius, bishop of Antioch and martyr, from the refutation [?] of Celsus, from the discourse on John, chapter 26. In various places Christ subordinates his own will to the will of the Father, or rather ratifies the Father's will above his own. This is not because there was a will in him that needed to be abolished. It was neither his divine will nor the will that belonged to his becoming man, for when he took on the nature he also took on what belongs to the nature. Rather, he was speaking to the Jews, who thought he was opposed to God the Father. So he said these things for the sake of the divine plan, saying, “I do not seek my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me.” From the impious Apollinarius, from the first discourse On the Union. Paul cries out most excellently, “In the almighty and only God we live and move and have our being.” So God's will alone was enough to give life and movement to the flesh through the Word who dwelt in it. The divine energy filled the place of the soul and of the human mind. This is also why John calls Christ's coming from heaven a “dwelling as in a tent.” For when he said that

“the Word became flesh,” he did not add “and soul.” Two beings that both have minds and wills cannot dwell together at once, or one would wage war against the other through its own will and activity. So the Word did not take hold of a human soul, but only of the seed of Abraham. The temple of Solomon had no soul, no mind and no will, and it prefigured the temple of Jesus' body. Such were the blasphemies of the God-hated Apollinarius, who called the Lord's flesh soulless and will-less. Eunomius the lawless and the Arianizers with him said the same. The new sophists have plainly pored over these men's theatrical books, have been pleased and delighted by them, and now draw up their battle lines against us. For Apollinarius himself says again, on “Father, let this cup pass from me; yet let not my will be done, but yours”: “If the one who was going to the passion and the cross was equal in power with the Father and shared in his essence, how could he pray in agony for the cup to pass him by, and ask that his own will not be done, but rather the Father's? And why did the will of the one praying need to be stated at all, unless it was out of harmony with God and contrary to him?” Gregory, the angel of the people of Nyssa, overturns these utterly godless ravings of Apollinarius in the writings he composed against him. He uses an argument of this kind: “Suppose the will of the one praying is done, that is, the will of the man understood to be in the Savior. Then he has been shown to have a will of his own, which refused death for the sake of the divine plan. Suppose instead that his will is not done. Even so his will has been done, for what he willed was that his will not be done. So whether the prayer is granted or not, Christ's human will was both shown and fulfilled.” From St Basil, from the discourse against the Arians

So he had one will with the Father, but he had also taken on the human will. For this reason he says, out of great abundance, “Let not my will be done, but yours.” From the same, from the same discourse. [?] being a partner and lifelong companion of the soul [?] and [?] of the life-giving and wholly immortal Word, and having from them as it were received the longing for immortality. From Ambrose, bishop of Milan, from the discourse on “Father, let this cup pass from me.” If the Savior refuses death according to his human will, do not be scandalized. For the flesh by nature had within itself the source of life and immortality, God the Word, and had as it were received a share in immortality. So it rightly turned away from death. It did so not out of cowardice but out of hatred for death, and because it was sinless and not subject to death.

From the same, from the same discourse. He was going to raise the whole of human nature from the tombs by his own voice, so how could he have been afraid of death? Rather, he was confirming his humanity against the unbelief of the heresies. For this reason, as he came to his passion, he used human deeds and human words. That is why he prays and sweats clots like blood. That is why the Maker of the angels is strengthened and given courage by an angel and asks for the cup to pass him by. And he bends his human will to his Father's divine will, saying, “Yet let not my will be done, but yours.” In this he shows not a division or opposition of wills, but his completeness as a man. For whoever accepts the nature certainly also makes what belongs to the nature his own. From St Athanasius, from the discourse on “The Lord created me” and against the Arians. And so, as he came to the cross, he prays earnestly and bends the knee, saying, “Father, let this cup pass from me; yet let not my will be done, but yours.” He calls the will of the flesh his own, since he also made our very flesh his own in himself. From Antipater, bishop of Bostra, from the discourse on the cross. For the refusal of death belonged to the human will of our nature in Christ, the will of which he says, “Let not my will be done, but yours.” As God he was foretelling that the cup would pass him by. For he rose on the third day, having made the flesh immortal and having crushed the [?] of death

From the same, from the same discourse against Apollinarius. He who suffered for us not only committed no sin, but also tore the roots of sin out from their foundations. So he does not say, “Let not my will be done,” as one opposed to God. He is giving us a pattern of how to pray to God in times of temptation. Apollinarius proclaims that Christ's incarnation was without soul and mind. On the grounds that Christ says, “Let not my will be done,” he does away with the rational part of his soul. But if that will, which loves life, is an insult to Christ, it is far more insulting to say that Christ became a curse and sin. The same goes for saying that he was tempted by Satan for forty days, fled from Herod into Egypt, was subject to Joseph the carpenter, and was strengthened by an angel as though he were afraid of death. From Ephrem, the most holy bishop of Antioch, from the third discourse against Severus. In the divine nature we speak of various properties of the nature: being uncreated, without beginning, unalterable, uncircumscribed and unchangeable, along with qualities that are akin and consonant with these and fit the divine essence alone. In the same way, in God's power of willing, the divine Scriptures say that God has many wills.

Think of the soul, which was made in God's image, in the same way. It too has in its essence one intellectual and rational power of desire. It received this power so that the divine commandments might be implanted in it and so that it might carry them out. As long as this power stays in accordance with nature, it is called neither sin nor righteousness, but a volitional disposition of the soul. From this self-determining power of the soul, then, come two kinds of will: the divine and the evil. When we turn our inclination toward God's commandment, our will is called divine. It is called this not because of its essence, but because of its action. When, on the other hand, it is dragged down into obedience to the evil one, it is rightly called a fleshly will. For example, to love life is a will that belongs to our rational nature. To live for our passions is a fleshly desire. And to despise and renounce life is a divine will. From the same, from the discourse on the apostolic saying that states, “He was tested in every way, apart from sin alone.” So the choir of the Fathers is seen to proclaim Christ perfect in divinity and perfect in humanity, consubstantial with us in every way, apart from sin alone. The bush at Sinai was a single, undivided substance, wholly wrapped in fire. The plant's foliage did not dim the fire's activity, and the activity of the flame did not harm the plant. In the same way, I ask you to understand that in the single person of Christ the divine and human properties exist without conflict [?]. And after other things: For this reason a likeness and prefiguration of the Son of God was depicted beforehand in the furnace of the youths. The human nature of those youths was almost wholly mingled with the activity and nature of the flame. Yet they walked about, moving from place to place by the activity of their bodies, and they sang their hymn by their intellectual will. The fire defiled none of the properties of their bodies or souls; Azariah was perfect both in fieriness and in humanity. In the same way we must understand that in Emmanuel the fire of his divinity was mingled with his soul and body like a breath of life. It sanctified them, yet it diminished none of the essential properties of the soul and body.

From Proclus, archbishop of Constantinople, from the discourse on the betrayal of Christ. “He began,” it says, “to be grieved and distressed.” Grief, distress and amazement are properties of a rational soul and belong to it by nature. The Savior's intellectual soul was free from sin alone. And after other things: When he said in his prayer, “Let not my will be done,” he showed himself to be truly a man, and by these words he signified his human will. And do not be amazed to see him allow his own flesh to be in agony over death. Something more lowly [?] than the agony is that after his resurrection he bore wounds

in his hands and side, and for forty days ate bodily and perishable food. From Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, from the discourse on the Nativity. For the Word delivered us from everything that came upon us through disobedience, and he cleansed our nature. But what he himself had made according to his own image needed no alteration. An example is the body that had been corrupted [?]: it was not corrupted along with it, but remained corruptible [?], as the soul is the image of God. From Olympiodorus, the great [?] philosopher of Alexandria, from the second discourse against Severus. After citing the passage of St Athanasius that speaks of the two wills in Christ, he goes on roughly as follows: “Severus regulates uprightness [?] by other rules. Not unreasonably [?], he distorted the present passage of the teacher, calling it an involuntary [?] reflection, in light of the Gospel words that come before and after it. Athanasius weighed these words by the same rule and applied to the Savior's humanity those that do not look toward the heights. So he is clearly also referring the will 'not wishing to die' to the one who was in the form of a man.” Interpretation of the citation. In the discourse against the Arians, in which the holy Athanasius [sets out] the two wills, he cited many Gospel passages of a lowly kind that fit Christ's humanity. Examples are “My Father is greater than I,” “Glorify me, Father,” “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified,” and “Jesus increased in wisdom and stature.” After citing all such passages, he took them and interpreted them of the Lord's flesh. Among them is also “Father, let this cup pass from me; yet let not my will be done, but yours.” Some say that when Christ says “not mine” he is not speaking about his own will, but about the will of a man subject to passions. Olympiodorus therefore wanted to show from the passages before and after that Athanasius understood “Let not my will” as referring to Christ's humanity. That is why he goes on [?] to say, “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.” Just as, then, we understand the spirit as Christ's, so also the flesh [?]. [?] on the prophetic saying about man that says to God, “You made him a little lower than the angels.” The Apostle refers this to Christ when he says, “But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels because of the suffering of death.” [?] a fleshly will, and they said another, a divine will. Chapter [?], in which the objections of the opponents are clearly [?] explained by us. Sayings of St Dionysius the Areopagite showing that [?] are clearly explained by us. 5. From St Dionysius the Areopagite: [sayings showing] that even apart from his humanity Christ has different activities according to the Word's [?]

[?] of the theandric activity in Christ, by Dionysius. Chapters that clearly show this: God the Word was hypostatically undivided in his own flesh and soul. Even so, he did not [?] suffer the properties of the flesh in his own nature, even though these properties were attributed to him most of all. Nor were they recognized as theandric, as the [?] claim. 6. A chapter that refutes the opponents who confess one simple nature in Christ [?] according to the laws of Mani [?]. It runs as follows: From Anastasius, presbyter and envoy of Rome, to the monks of Ascalon. “I have perceived that your pious brotherly love is eagerly disposed toward learning the divine doctrines,” and so on. Various doctrinal texts follow. From John [?], on the natural and blameless passions. “We confess that our Lord Jesus Christ took on all the natural and blameless passions of man, [except] sin. For sin is not natural, and the Creator did not sow it in us. It comes about voluntarily in our free choice from what the devil sows, and it does not rule us by force,” and so on. Again [?]: a refutation of the Monophysites' proposition that says the perfect [?] incarnate hypostasis of God the Word, and that in it the whole fullness of the Trinity is seen, and so on. Difficulties and examinations in the form of question and answer: that foreknowledge and will are not the same thing, and that foreknowledge according to will is not the cause of what is foreknown concerning vice and virtue. Question of the opponents. Answer of the Orthodox. From Anastasius of Sinai, on where blasphemy comes from. It begins: “Brothers, the human soul often speaks within itself certain shameful and impure thoughts, godless blasphemies and unseemly words against God and the holy, life-giving and awesome mys[teries]…” OF OUR HOLY FATHER

ANASTASIUS OF SINAI: A VERY PROFITABLE DISCOURSE ON THOSE WHO HAVE FALLEN ASLEEP. Why have we gathered today, beloved, both earnestly and fittingly? The brothers who have been called from among us to Christ have called us all together. So let us come eagerly to Christ in hymnody (1). Those who have left us in the flesh have roused us to give glory on earth on their behalf. They give glory with the angels in heaven and stand in their choirs. They are filled with the delights of paradise, and they have set a spiritual table before us (2). They enjoy the consolation of that place, and they have set before us the wine of compunction. They lit up their own hearts and journeyed toward the light that never sets, and they have lit lamps for us. For the holy ones who are with Christ have drawn the holy ones away from us. Those who were once with us have departed from us. They have left us orphans and gone on foot to their own homeland. They have left corruption behind and gone on to incorruption. They have set, departing from (3) [?] the world, toward Christ. [?] as just below, “have set wine before us.”

from the world, and have risen toward Christ. They have gone out of their tent and come to dwell in the Jerusalem above. They have left us in the vanity of this life and reached the (4) blessedness above. They have left us amid empty tumults and journeyed to places free of tumult. They have come out of the storm and surge of the world and put into harbors of perfect calm. Even when they were with us, they were not with us; they kept their minds on God. While they were on earth, their citizenship was in heaven. They had no lasting city here, only the heavenly one (5). They had no passing wealth here, only the heavenly (6) wealth. They were strangers (7) and sojourners, as their fathers were too. They were strangers to the world, to the things in the world and to worldly ways. With their whole soul they looked to the things above in heaven. They set their minds on the things above and meditated on them. They longed for the beauties of that place, its dwellings and tents, the choirs (8) above, the hymns above, the feasts there and the everlasting good things. They looked toward these things, they gazed at them, they ran toward them, and so they attained them. They hurried, and so they entered (9) the bridal chamber and the wedding hall. They toiled, and so they rejoice. They were not careless, and so they exult. They went out and departed to the holy and eternal land. They went out and departed on their way, the good way that is pleasing to God. They went out suddenly and flew away (10) like sweet-voiced swallows. They flew off like solitary, wholly pure turtledoves. They have left the fold, and the sheep are downcast. They have left our nest, and we fledglings cry out. One limb has been cut off, and the other limbs are in pain. This is why we weep: we have been deprived of your goodness. We groan, because we no longer see your faces. We lament, because we have been bereaved so suddenly. We are downcast whenever we remember your virtue, whenever we look around and do not see your love. We weep, because even animals weep when separated from their own kind, and even oxen low as they search for their yokemate. Even if this happened for your benefit, you have left us disheartened. For you it was something to desire, but for us (11) it is grievous. For “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones,” but the death of us sinners is evil. That is why the Prophet also said, “Why (15) should I fear on the evil day? The iniquity of my heel has surrounded me.” [?] the morning they did not reach [?]. For whoever does not reach the summit of [?] poverty, let him manage well the wealth gathered unjustly. For we have here no lasting city, but the one to come. (6) Heavenly wealth [?] here I think [?]

For our hour and our day will come too, brothers. It will surely come, and it will not pass us by: the hour when a man will leave everything behind and depart alone. He will go solitary, humbled, naked, helpless, unprotected, unaccompanied, unprepared and without confidence, if it overtakes him in his negligence on a day he does not know and at an hour he does not expect. While he lives in luxury, while he indulges himself, while he prospers, while he is free of care, a single hour will suddenly come, and everything has stopped. A slight fever, and everything comes to nothing. A little pain, and all is empty and vain. One deep, dark and painful night, and he is led away like a condemned man, wherever those who lead him take him. Then, O man, you will need many guides. You will need many helpers, many prayers and many fellow workers in the hour when the soul is separated. Great is the fear then, and great the trembling. Great is the mystery and great the crisis, because we are going to the place from which no one has returned. It is the one hour, and there is no other hour; the one road, and there is no other road; the one bridge, and there is no way around it. It is the end of all and the toll that all must pay. Hard is the crossing, but we all cross over by it. Bitter is the cup, but we all drink it and no other. Great and hidden is the mystery of death, and no one can describe it to us. Terrible and fearful are the things the soul then undergoes, but none of us knows them, except only those who have gone ahead to that place, who have crossed over there, who have had the experience. Tell me, do you not see it when we sit beside our brothers as they die or breathe their last? Do we not see fearful things then? We see how they hold on, how they are troubled, how they groan, how they sweat a cold and bitter sweat like reapers in a field; how some grind their teeth while others are struck with amazement and troubled; how they leap up from the bed, wanting to flee but unable. For they see what they have never seen, they hear from the powers what they have never heard, and they suffer what they have never suffered. They look for someone to rescue them, they look for someone to comfort them, and there is no one who dares. When we see them, we tremble and weep. We hold their hands and embrace them, we wet them with our tears, we wipe the sweat from their faces, we wipe away their [?] (Note: “Our hour”: so I have printed it, instead of “the day.”)

…do not be afraid, God is helping you, for he loves mankind.” These are the things we say to him. We wet our breasts with tears and our hearts burn within us. In that moment there is no evil desire in us, no thought of money, no care for food. We see the great and fearful mystery of death, and we tremble. Shaking our heads, we bewail ourselves: “Woe to us, what has happened! Into what evils we have fallen through our disobedience! Into what [?]… O wretched life! ‘You are earth, and to earth you shall return.’ O most bitter sentence, which no one can escape!” Then the one who is departing kisses us all and says: “Farewell, my good brothers, farewell, and pray earnestly for me in this hour. I am now setting out on a long road that I have truly never walked, into a foreign land where no one knows me, into a fearful world from which no one has returned, into the dark place where I do not know what will meet me, into deep Hades from which no one has come back up. So then, fare you well, my beloved brothers, fare you well. From now on I am no longer your brother. Fare you well, friends, for I am no longer a friend but a stranger. Farewell, fair choir that sang together; but it is no longer a song sung together, it is a lament. Fare you well, my kin, who are now strangers to me. Farewell for a little while; then come, leave everything behind. We are waiting for you to come to us, for we no longer come to you. Whatever we have seen, we have seen; whatever we have done, we receive back. Now whatever good I have done, that I have gained, and whatever I have sent on ahead, that will meet me. If I have shown mercy to anyone, it will help me in this hour, for this present hour of the soul is narrow and heavy for me beyond every other hour. Oh, what shall I do, wretch that I am? I have been caught unprepared. Dark for me is the present night, for I have been cut down without fruit. But weep bitterly for me and lament. Have pity, O [?], have compassion and help me. Feel for me and pray, so that I may find a little forgiveness there, so that I may receive a little mercy there. I do not ask for much, because I have sinned much. Alas, how I deceived myself! How I mocked myself, saying: ‘I am still young; for now I will enjoy the things of [?]. I will revel in the world. I will pamper my flesh, and later I will repent.’ [?] for it is the…

…day after day I wasted my own life in wickedness! I was taught, and paid no heed. I was admonished, and laughed. I heard the Scriptures as though I did not hear them. I heard about the judgment, and sneered. I heard about death, and behaved as though I were immortal, and scorned it as though I would live forever. And see, I have been overtaken unrepentant, and there is no one to redeem me. See, I beg

and there is no one who listens. Truly the judgment of God is just. How often I promised him that I would repent, and then did worse things again! How often he had mercy on me, and I provoked him again!” While the dying man keeps saying these things to us who are present, suddenly his tongue is bound, his mind [?], and his eyes change, when at last the powers of the Master arrive. For the pitiless collectors seize us and drag us off to the tribunal. When the wretched man sees them, whether he is a king, a ruler or a tyrant, he is shaken through and through, and the whole house trembles as if from an earthquake. He trembles all over, he is all troubled, all amazed and beside himself, for he sees fearful powers, strange and mighty forms, an array such as he has never beheld. These are the things the one being led away then sees; he no longer sees us, but he is stunned and beside himself before the powers that summon him. Perhaps he even whispers some entreaties to them, as far as his tongue is able to speak. From his words and his manner we who are present often understand that he has seen the Master's powers. Then all of us, seized with trembling, shudder and nod to one another, saying: “Let us pray, brothers, for he stands in a great contest. Let us take heed and think about this hour.” For what is man? Nothing. What is man? A worm and ashes, a shadow and a dream. See, he has passed on; see, he has gone away; see, he has come to rest; see, he has fallen silent. That man of great renown, the … (Notes: Συνετασσόμην: “I promised.” Συνετασσόμην: “I promised.” Ὁρῶν τάξιν: that is, ranks. Σύντρομοι: that is, trembling. Ὁ πολύς: very renowned; see Synesius, vol. II. Τόπῳ: in which.)

…so that we may not be suddenly snatched away before we are ready. Let us go in, so that we may not be left outside. Let us put away those vain sluggish ways. Let us put away the slackness in which we have lived until now. Let us cast off the hopes that mock us day after day. From now on, let not that foul and wicked thought deceive us. For many who made many plans for tomorrow did not live to see it, but were suddenly snatched away like a sparrow by a hawk, like a lamb by a wolf, unable to speak at all or to make their wills. Some who went to sleep healthy in the evening did not live to see the morning. Others breathed their last while sitting at table. Others were walking about, fell, and suddenly died. All these things we have seen and we know. Therefore we have no excuse before God, because we go astray not in ignorance but in knowledge: we hear the divine Scriptures and understand what they say, but we do not do it. So I urge you: let us be not only hearers of the teaching but also doers. If anyone who had an evil habit of fornication has cut it off after hearing what has just been said, he is a good hearer. If anyone who held a grudge against his neighbor is reconciled to him, he is a good hearer. If anyone, pierced to the heart by these words, becomes merciful and generous, he is a good hearer. Otherwise this reading too may turn into a judgment against us, for we hear and do not do. If your brother's death does not bring you to your senses, no one can help you. If you do not repent when you look at a corpse, when will you ever turn back? If you were not pierced to the heart by what has just been said, when will you depart from sin? This practice of the divine oracles, beloved, our brothers who have gone before us to Christ have handed on to us. They prepared these life-giving foods for us. They mixed for us this wine of teaching, so that by meditating on these things by night and by day, in church and at home, at table and in bed, we may be able to turn away from our evil and vain habits and our negligence, to turn our soul and bend it to repentance, even if only from now on, to entreat the Master, and to attain the kingdom of heaven, by the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ. For to him belongs glory, with the Father who has no beginning and the life-giving and Holy Spirit, now and always and to the endless ages of ages. Amen. (Notes: περιεζήσασεν: perhaps περιεζήσαμεν, or παρεζήσαμεν. Ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ: perhaps he had written ἡμέρᾳ …)

DISPUTATION OF ABBA ANASTASIUS AGAINST THE JEWS

Before anything else, the Christian should ask the Jew this: “Why are you called Jew, Hebrew and Israelite? And what is the meaning of the three names?” When the Jew answers, “I am called Hebrew after Abraham, Jew after Judah, and Israelite because Jacob was called Israel by God,” say to him: “That is not what I asked you. I want you to tell me what Jew, Hebrew and Israelite mean.” If he can tell you, say to him, “That is why your name is Jew,” and then begin on what is to be said below from the testimonies of the prophets. But if he cannot tell you, do not say a word to him except this: “Go and learn what you are called, and then come back and I will talk with you about your faith.” The meaning of the three names is this. Hebrew means “one who crosses over,” that is, one who passes through, because he crossed the Jordan and the sea. Jew means “confession.” Israelite means “a mind that sees God,” since they knew God before all the nations. Abraham too means “one who crosses over,” since he crossed the Jordan from Mesopotamia. Jerusalem means “vision of peace,” and Sabaoth means “peacemaker,” “Lord of hosts.” Mount Sinai means “mountain of the bush”; Sinai means “bush.” Moses means in Egyptian “ark, water and wood,” since he was found in the water in a wooden ark. Aaron means “mountainous.” Salem means “place of God.” [?] means in the Saracen tongue “I saw him.” John means “in whom is grace” and “obedient to the Lord,” since he was to run ahead and proclaim the Lord. Jesus means “savior.” Bethlehem means “house of bread,” since there the heavenly bread, Christ our Lord, was born. Jordan means “his descent,” since the Lord came down and was baptized himself

…Christ, the Son of the living God, the salvation of Christians, the overthrow of Jews and Greeks, the destruction of idols.

Then, once the Jew has admitted that he knows what you asked earlier, begin by speaking to him like this: “O Jew, what I am about to tell you is not said by us alone; your own Scriptures bear witness to the same things and say them. To whom, then, did God say, ‘Let us make man in our image and in our likeness’?” If he says, “To the angels,” say to him: “How can that be? I tell you that he said this to the Son. You refuse to accept the One, and so you bring in countless others; you reject the Son, and so you attach the dignity of counselor to servants and make our fellow servants lords over our creation. Tell me, is it not man who, perfected by a good way of life, is raised to the dignity of the angels? And what creature can be equal to its Creator? Consider also what follows: ‘In our image.’ What do you say to this? Is there one image shared by God and the angels? By no means. But the Son and the Father must necessarily have the same form, the form being understood, of course, in a way befitting God: not as a bodily shape but as the distinctive property of the Godhead. Listen to what he says: ‘In our image.’ To whom else, if not to the radiance of his glory and the imprint of his substance, his Son and Word, who is the image of the invisible God? So it is to his own living Image, which said, ‘I and the Father are one,’ and, ‘Whoever has seen me has seen the Father,’ that he says, ‘Let us make man in our image.’ Where there is one image, where is the unlikeness? Then: ‘And God made man,’ not ‘they made.’ The text avoided a plurality of persons. By saying, ‘Let us make man,’ it instructs you, the Jew; by saying, ‘And God made man,’ it shuts out paganism. It returned safely to the unity, so that you might understand the Son together with the Father and escape the danger of polytheism. And when it says, ‘And he breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul,’ is it not plain that it was showing the divine working of the Holy Spirit? This was proclaimed through the prophets too, as in: ‘The Spirit of the Lord is upon me’; and, ‘The Spirit of the Lord guided them’; and, ‘The Spirit of understanding filled Bezalel,’ the master builder of the tabernacle; and, ‘the Spirit that was provoked’; and, ‘the Spirit that took Elijah up in a chariot and was sought in double measure by Elisha’; and David was guided and strengthened by a good and princely Spirit. The Spirit was promised earlier by Joel, who says, ‘And in the last days I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh’—that is, on the flesh that has believed—‘and on your sons

and on your daughters,’ and so on. And: ‘The divine Spirit made me, and the breath of the Almighty teaches me.’ And again: ‘You will send forth your Spirit and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth.’ In the same way, when God says of Adam, ‘See, Adam has become like one of us,’ he indicates Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Count this too, and look at what is said about God through the Law: ‘Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God, the Lord is one.’ Is it not evident from this threefold expression that the Holy Trinity is one God? That Father, Son and Holy Spirit are one God is clear both from what has been said and from what we have still to say. Pay attention here as well. We call him the Son of whom the prophet said, ‘By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm.’ And what do we call the Holy Spirit? ‘And by the Spirit of his mouth all their host.’ For this is how we worship one God in Trinity. Now you tell me, O Jew: to whom does your Scripture say, ‘The Lord said to me, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you”’?” If he says that the psalm is speaking about Solomon, say to him: “And how much of the world did Solomon rule? Clearly not half of the world, nor even a third, but only Judea. Listen carefully, O Jew, and learn that the psalm speaks about Christ and not about Solomon. For it says: ‘The Lord said to me, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession. You will shepherd them with a rod of iron; you will shatter them like a potter's vessels.”’ So tell me now, Jew: it is perfectly clear and agreed, as we said, that Solomon held neither half the earth nor a third of it, but only the land of Judea. When, then, did Solomon possess the ends of the earth? When did he shepherd them with a rod of iron? When did he shatter his enemies like a potter's vessels? Never at all.” But the Jew may say: “If he is the Son of God, as you claim, how could God say to him, as to a servant, ‘Ask of me, and I will give you’? And again, ‘Today I have begotten you’? He speaks as to a servant, it seems, because of the asking and receiving, and as to a creature of a day, because of ‘Today I have begotten you.’ Yet you Christians say that he was begotten before the whole world.” If he says this, answer him thus: “As for the Father saying to the Son, ‘Ask of me, and I will give you,’ do not be scandalized. A king, too, often says to his own son out of great love, ‘Ask of me, and I will give you whatever you want.’ And as for ‘Today I have begotten you,’ he is speaking of his birth according to the flesh, for by the good pleasure of the Father he was born of the holy Theotokos and ever-virgin Mary. For to which of the angels did he ever say,

‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’? Are they not all ministering spirits sent out to serve? And again, elsewhere: ‘I will be a Father to him, and he will be a Son to me.’ He said these things with reference to his humanity and his incarnate dispensation. They do not show his eternal birth, but the birth joined to time. For he who is Son of God by nature also became man by nature for our salvation, not receiving sonship by grace. (He has it by nature, and as man he receives again what he had as God. For being Most High, he became God [?].) As God he was always Master of all things; as man he took on the glory that he had as God. He asked, not to receive what he did not have, but that what he had might be revealed. As it is written: ‘You will shepherd them with a rod of iron,’ which is the empire of the Romans. Christ the Son of God gave this empire to faithful and Christian emperors, and he presides over it and reigns together with them. Through him the faithful nations, allotted to him as a possession, are shepherded [?] to believe in him. That is why all the nations that clash with the empire of the Christians, even if they are defeated, have not displaced it and never will. As it is written in the Book of Psalms about the kingdom of Christ: ‘My truth and my mercy are with him, and in my name his horn will be exalted. I will set his hand on the sea and his right hand on the rivers. He will call upon me, “You are my Father, my God, and the helper of my salvation.” And I will make him firstborn, high above the kings of the earth. Forever I will keep my mercy for him, and my covenant will stand firm with him. I will establish his seed forever and ever, and his throne like the days of heaven. If his sons forsake my law’—that is, the Christians—‘and do not walk in my judgments, if they profane my statutes and do not keep my commandments, I will punish their transgressions with the rod and their iniquities with scourges. But I will not scatter my mercy from them, nor will I break my covenant. Once for all I have sworn by my holiness; will I lie to David? His seed endures forever’—and that seed is Christ, the seed of David according to the flesh—‘and his throne is like the sun before me, and like the moon established forever, and the witness in heaven is faithful.’ And so that you, a Jew, may not suppose that these things were said about David and his kingdom, that is, the Jews, rather than about Christ, the psalm goes on to describe what happened: David died, the kingdom of the Jews passed away, and the old covenant was profaned. It says: ‘But you have rejected and scorned and cast off your anointed one. You have overturned the covenant of your servant; you have profaned his sanctuary to the ground. You have torn down all

…his hedges, along with the rest, and you have poured shame upon him.” And truly the Holy Spirit spoke these things well through the prophet. For it is impossible for God to lie, but by an oath he guaranteed that his truth cannot change, as it is said: “Once I have sworn by my truth: shall I lie to David?” For Christ the Son of God is the seed of David according to the flesh. The Theotokos, the Ever-Virgin Mother of Christ our God, was of the line of David according to the flesh, and the kingdom that he received as man remains forever. David died and was buried, and his kingdom, the kingdom of the Jews, was taken away. But the kingdom that God promised to give to Christ our God made flesh, in his humanity, remains forever. He has entrusted it to faithful emperors and reigns together with them, as we said, for there is no other kingdom or dominion more glorious than this. If you want to examine the matter precisely, take for me the people of Moses, who with so many signs sent the Egyptians down into the depths of the sea. Look at Joshua the son of Nun, at whose word the sun stood still over Gibeon and the moon over the valley, along with other extraordinary wonders. In short, consider the whole power of the Hebrews. Did they not reign for a thousand years, and then their kingdom was cut off? How? Was it not by the kingdom of the Romans [?]? Did not Titus and Vespasian cut them all down, and lay the temple waste with the plough? Was not the kingdom of the Babylonians, of the Medes, of the Persians swallowed up by these barbarians, the Turks? But they too will be cut off. Did not the kingdom of the Macedonians pass away? But the kingdom of the Romans, that is, of the Christians, will not pass away until the end of the world, since our Lord Jesus Christ reigns together with it. As King of those who reign and Lord of those who rule, he shepherds his people through it until his second coming, and it will not be left to another people. Then he will hold it as Father of the age to come, when we all rise again, as it is written: “The dead will rise, and those in the tombs will be raised up.” We shall stand before the judgment seat of his impartial judgment, and he will scatter his enemies into Hades to be punished eternally: those, that is, who did not want to believe in him now and to have him reign over them. But those who believed and faithfully kept his commandments will reign with him forever, as Solomon says in Proverbs: “And the Lord will reign over them forever.” “And behold, one was coming with the clouds of heaven, and he came to the Ancient of Days. To him were brought the honor and the kingdom, and all the tribes will serve him. His (Mic. 4:7)

kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and his authority is to generations and years, and it will not pass away.” But if you say, O Jew, “Christ has not yet come, but he will come toward the last times,” what will be left for him to do when time itself is being brought to an end? Perhaps you will say, “To restore what has been destroyed, that is, the nation of the Jews.” But how does it make sense for him to create anew what is destroyed by his own command and will? Such a tale is incoherent. Nowhere is it said that after the dissolution of this world another such establishment of the Jews will arise again. What the prophet does tell you is this: “I will send you Elijah the Tishbite before the great day of the Lord comes, lest I come and strike the earth utterly.” If this one whom you expect as Christ is Elijah, who comes not to restore but to strike, then notice that he is not called Christ but Elijah. He is not born in Bethlehem, as the prophet declared to you, but born in Thisbe. For the one who said “I will send you Elijah” is other than the one who is sent. And when he said “lest I come and strike the earth utterly,” he means that he first bears witness through that man, that is, Elijah, and then takes away everything that now exists, that is, brings about the end. What use would it be, then, for Christ to be born at that time? Whom would he please or serve once the end has come? Christ is one person and Elijah another. The prophet Daniel saw him, for the king of the Babylonians, as a stone that also became a great mountain. For he says this: “And in the days of those kings God will raise up a kingdom that will never be destroyed, and it,” he says, “will stand forever.” And: “The king saw that a stone was cut out of a mountain without hands and struck the image; and the stone became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.” By the four kings he means the glorious and famous kingdoms: of the Babylonians, of the Medes, and third the predatory and formidable Macedonian kingdom of Alexander, that is, of the Greeks. These are the three mighty ones, and this fourth is the bold one counted together with the three. After these kingdoms this one was found, the kingdom of Christ, which Daniel called unconquered and without successor [?]. And if you say it is the iron kingdom of Augustus Caesar, whom did the kingdom of Augustus and of the other emperors grind to powder or subdue for good? They both conquered and were conquered. Even if they conquered you Jews and many other nations, they were defeated in their turn, and the rule of Augustus Caesar passed away. But the kingdom of Christ will have no end forever. For what grinds to powder remains unconquered, untamed and without successor, and that is the name and the kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ, and our faith in him. How many pagans and heretical emperors and nations have made war on the faith of us

Christians, and could not extinguish it? They perished and passed away, but our faith shines and spreads every day. If you want to learn the exact time, take the words “In those days God will raise up a kingdom” as referring to the kingdom that appeared in the midst of them, that is, of the four kingdoms described; for afterwards it will not be found. Just as your fathers clung to an expectation that had already passed and fell away from this opportunity, so do you. If, then, you believe that there is a Christ, seek him from this point on; for afterwards [you will] not

I have already shown, O Jew, from the Scriptures and from the truth itself, that the words “The Lord said to me: You are my Son, today I have begotten you,” and “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance,” and what follows, were spoken about the incarnate dispensation of the Son of God. These things also came to pass and are witnessed by the truth itself and by your own prophets. If you wish, I will show you that he was also begotten before the world, and that Christ is God. But first I want to learn from you: David, who was both king and prophet, whom did he have as Lord and Master? It is entirely clear and agreed that he had no Lord except the one who made heaven and earth. Look, then: David himself says about Christ that he is his Lord, and that he was begotten before the ages. David did not ascend into heaven, yet he himself says in the book of Psalms, namely Psalm 109: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand.” See, then, he calls the Son of God his Lord. For the Father said to him, after his holy birth according to the flesh from the Virgin, his saving passion, his resurrection from the dead and his ascension: “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.” But perhaps you will say, O Jew, that Christ sits at the right hand of God until he makes the last, appointed coming that he promised through the prophets, as though he had not yet come. How does that make sense, tell me? Why does he say “Sit” again to one who is already sitting? And against whom were the enemies hostile, if he had not yet come? For in saying “Sit,” he tells the one who ascended from earth to heaven to be seated again, as he was before, above his enemies. So you Jews are his enemies, trampled under the feet of the Christian race until the last hour. Hence you are justly trampled, and what will befall you is just. For the time you speak of and await is granted to overtake you swifter than a glance [?], and after it you who believe a deceiver are handed over to the expectation of eternal fire. And again the same prophet and king, in the same psalm, speaking as in the person of God the Father

says this about the Son and Word of God: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” The morning star was made on the fourth day, but Adam was formed on the sixth day. So tell me, O Jew, whom did God beget before he prepared the creation? Do you mean Adam? Not at all, for he was formed two days after the morning star and the stars. Is it speaking to you about the Anointed? But do you not say that he is the son of David? And David was born many ages after Adam, for Adam was formed on the sixth day, as was said, and the morning stars were made on the fourth day. Yet God says about his own Son: “Before the morning star I begot you,” and “a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek,” that is, a priest of the nations. For Melchizedek offered wine and bread to God, just as Christ our high priest handed down to us the offering of bloodless sacrifices to him according to the order of Melchizedek. Hear also Solomon speaking of the birth of the only-begotten Son of God before the ages: “Before the mountains came to be, before the springs came forth, before all the hills, he begets me.” Show me, then, whom God begot before all creation. Likewise David again says in the book of Psalms, Psalm 71: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king's son.” And do not say that he is speaking about Solomon, for a few verses later he says: “He will have dominion from sea to sea, and his name endures before the sun and before the moon, for generations of generations.” See, I have shown you clearly, through both David and Solomon, that the Son was begotten of the Father before all creation, in a way that he alone knows. Again, tell me this, and the truth will appear at once: the Anointed one whom you await, what do you say he is? God, or a mere man like David and the rest of mankind? The Jew may say: “We say he is a man and not God, one like the prophets. For there is only one God, not two, as you Christians say.” Since you say that your coming Christ is a mere man, let us now bring forward the words of the prophets. If they proclaimed the one who was to come as God, then clearly the one who came, and who is worshiped and believed in by us Christians, is truly the true Christ, while the one whom you Jews await is a deceiver and the Antichrist. But if we do not produce prophets who call him God, then clearly we are in error and the Jews are telling the truth. Tell me of whom the prophet speaks: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; God is Lord, and he has appeared to us.” Pay close attention: he plainly says God and Lord when he says, “God and Lord, and he has appeared to us.” So whether he has appeared to us or is yet to appear, he is not the Christ of you Jews, but ours,

the Christians'. For you await the one who is to come as a mere man and not as God, but David proclaimed the one who was to come, and who has come, as God and Lord. Isaiah says: “Not an angel, not an envoy, but the Lord himself will come and save us.” And: “A child is born to us, a son is given to us, and he is called Angel of great counsel, Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Ruler, Prince of peace, Father of the age to come.” How can a man, as you say, be “Mighty God, Ruler, Prince of peace, Father of the age to come”? Likewise Habakkuk says: “God will come from Teman.” Hear Jeremiah too, crying aloud: “This is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him. He found out every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel whom he loved. After this he appeared on earth and lived among men.” Do you see that they proclaimed as true [God?] the one who appeared on earth and lived among men? And David says of him: “God has become king over the nations,” that is, by drawing them to God through faith in his Son. Why did he not say, “God has become king over the Jews”? And again: “All the nations have seen the salvation of our God.” And: “Say among the nations that the Lord has become king,” that is, through faith. And Isaiah: “From the rising of the sun to its setting my name is glorified among the nations.” And again Hosea: “God says: I will call those who were not my people my people,” that is, the nations, “and her who was shown mercy, not shown mercy,” that is, the synagogue of the Jews. Likewise the patriarch Jacob, when he blessed his sons and gave them his final instructions, said this about Christ: “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until he comes for whom it is reserved,” that is, Christ, “and he is the expectation of the nations,” since he knew the hardness of the Jews. So the Jews expect in vain the one they expect. For the Christ whom the nations expect has come, and that is why the ruler from Judah has failed, and

That Christ is true and not a deceiver, as you Jews say and think, let us prove to you as well, not by words only but by deeds that cry out and bear witness to this day throughout the whole inhabited world, showing that everything he said has come to pass. For he said: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away.” Listen attentively to which words. He said about your temple, the temple of the Jews: “Truly I tell you, not one stone will be left upon another in it.” Has his word been fulfilled upon it, or not? He said that

“The Romans will come and take away your nation and the city and the kingdom.” Did this come about under Vespasian and Titus, or not? He said that “The law and the prophets were until John the Baptist, and they will cease.” Has this not come about? What prophet have you had after John the Baptist? Show me, then: since you crucified Christ, what prophet has been found among you? What kingdom do you have today? Where are your judges? Where are your rulers? They have all failed. Where is your temple? See, it lies desolate. Where are the tablets that you [received?]? See, they are no more. Where are your sacrifices? See, they have ceased. Where is the ark of the covenant? See, it is nowhere to be seen. Where is the altar that Moses made? Where is the rod that budded? Where are the jar and the manna? Where is the overshadowing in the temple and the purification of the sanctuary? Where is the fire that came down from heaven? Where do you have a single prophet today? In truth you have none, according to the voice of the three young men, which speaks on your behalf: “At this time there is no ruler, prophet or leader,” and what follows, “before God, and to find mercy.” Which of the places that God gave you do you have today? He took them all from you and gave them to us. Even if you mention Sinai, where you received the law and yet did not accept it, Christ is glorified there today. Even if you mention the Jordan, where your people crossed in those days, Christ was baptized there, and he is glorified there by us. Even if you mention Jerusalem and Zion, Christ was crucified there, and his sufferings are venerated there today. Or if you mention the Mount of Olives, Christ was taken up from there, and he is glorified there. Even if you mention Bethlehem, the city of David, Christ was born there, and he is glorified there always, as in heaven. But why do I speak of Bethlehem and Zion and the Jordan? Travel through the West, survey the East, search out all that is under heaven, even the British Isles themselves, the westernmost and farthest parts of the world: the things of the Jews and the pagans have grown old and vanished, but the things of Christ are everywhere believed, honored and confirmed. And do not say that Christians today are oppressed and taken captive. This is the great thing: that although our faith is persecuted and warred against by so many, it stands and does not cease, our empire is not abolished, and our churches are not closed. In the midst of the nations that rule and persecute us we have churches, we set up crosses, we build churches and we offer sacrifices. He said: “The Gospel will be preached in the whole world.” Has it come about or not? He said that the gates of Hades will not prevail against his Church, that is, our faith. Did he lie? Were there not pagans, and many heresiarchs, and powerful tyrants, and impious emperors who made war on our faith, and were not able (John 11:48. Luke 16:16. Dan. 3:[?])

to extinguish it? He said to us who believe in him: “You will be hated by all because of my name.” Now tell us, Jews: is it not because of the name of Christ that all the nations hate and abhor us? Even if you pass over all these things in silence, the stones will cry out. We see that since the beginning of the world no nation has been found that was warred against by all for so many years and yet not wiped out, except the nation of the Christians alone. It would not have survived, warred against in this way by all the nations, if the hand of the Lord had not guarded it, and did not still guard it, from being wiped out. And another thing: no Christian emperor has ever been handed over to death by barbarians, even though so many nations have made war on the empire. And not only could they not destroy the emperor; they could not even abolish his image, together with the cross, from the coinage, although some tyrants attempted it. Do not think this a slight or trivial matter, that our faith has never ceased to be warred against and yet stands and is not wiped out. If God had not chosen and loved our faith above all others, he would not have kept it unconquered among the nations, who are like wolves. Moreover, God would never have allowed an erring faith to hold dominion over all the ends of the earth, if there had not been the dispensation of the incarnate coming of Christ, his Son, our God and Savior. Hence the very fact that the Gospel of Christ has been believed among all the nations is the most unerring testimony that there is no more pious faith under heaven. Is God so unjust? Far from it! If he had known that we Christians were in error, would he have left us like this? Consider how many years have passed since Christ: [would he let] so great a race and multitude of people perish in error? And do not look at this or say that we are now being chastised for so many years by the Ishmaelite [text: Israelite] nations. Rather, explain this to me: how did God entrust the kingdom of the whole earth to us, who are in error, as you say? How is it that no one has been able to abolish the stamp on the gold coinage or take it away from us? How many kings of the nations, Persians and Arabs, attempted this and were utterly unable? This was so that God might show that, even if we Christians are persecuted, we nevertheless reign over all. For the sign on the gold coinage of our empire is the sign of Christ himself. Tell me: if this were not a sign that the faith and the empire of the Christians are eternal, invincible and indelible, how is it that all of you, who hate and blaspheme the cross of Christ, have fallen away [?]? How is it that you cannot erase the cross from the gold, but even accept it eagerly, and if you see a gold coin without a cross you abhor it and turn away from it? David spoke well about you: “Eye-

…they have eyes, and will not see; they have hearts, and do not understand.” How is it that you long for the very thing you fight against, and eagerly accept the very thing you abhor, defeated against all expectation? If you had any sense and understanding, this one sign would be enough, for you and for everyone, to show and convince you that the faith and the cross of Christ reign always, forever. How many have tried to destroy our faith and the Church, and could not? They have passed away, but the foundation of the Church and the faith stand unshaken because of Christ, who decreed: “The gates of Hades shall not prevail against it.” Where is Diocletian? Where is Nero? Where is Vespasian? Where is Herod? Where is Maximian, and all who killed the martyrs of Christ but could neither stop our faith nor shut it down? They perished and came to nothing. Christ did not lie to us when he said, “You will be hated by all for my name’s sake,” and again, “You will be brought before kings and governors for my sake.” So take your pick: if you hate us, you really show that Christ told us the truth when he said, “You will be hated by all for my name’s sake.” And not only this: he said many other things as well, which we see happening every day, and so we worship him as God all the more. He said that his Gospel would be preached in the whole world. He said, “Not one stone shall be left upon another in your temple.” He said, “Whoever does not leave father and brothers and sisters cannot follow me.” He told us to give alms in secret. He told us, “Be baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” He told us, “I am with you always, to the end of the age.” Who, then, can prove that Christ lied when he said these things? No one at all. Everything has come to pass, as we said, and is still coming to pass. Has your temple not fallen and been burned? Has his Gospel not been preached in the whole world? Are we Christians not hated by all the nations for his name? Do we not see countless people leaving fathers and mothers to follow Christ? Do we not see and understand that Christ is with us always, to the end of the age, and does not allow our faith to be abolished? Who, then, seeing so many such words and deeds of his, which he foretold eight hundred years ago or more, coming to pass and shining forth today and every day, can disbelieve him or stumble over him? God forbid! So anyone who wishes can learn from this that there is no more pious faith on earth than faith in Christ alone. To him be glory and might. Amen.

SECOND QUESTION BY THE SAME AUTHOR. The prophets proclaimed beforehand everything concerning him, but you do not look. Perhaps you say: “If our prophets spoke about Christ, why did they not tell us openly and explicitly, ‘Know, you Jews, that Christ is going to come and abolish the law and the sacrifices of the law’?” I tell you that if they had put the matter so baldly, you would at once have stoned them and burned their books. And so in this we are now well served [?]: for we now put you to shame from your own prophets, refuting you with them and demonstrating everything about Christ from them. David says: “He bowed the heavens and came down.” Isaiah says: “Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel.” There is the birth. And again the same prophet says: “This is our God; no other shall be compared with him,” and “afterward he appeared on earth and lived among men.” There is his life among men. And there was no other way for him to be seen by men, or to live among them in bare divinity, except by putting on and clothing himself with human nature and flesh. After Moses had seen the glory of God, so that the children of Israel could not look at his uncovered face unless he put on the veil, he said to them: “The Lord our God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers.” What does “like me” mean? Just as Moses’ face was glorified, and because the children of Israel could not gaze at its glory he put a veil over his face and only then spoke with them, so Christ, the Son of God, took the temple of the body as his covering, hiding his divinity, and became mediator between God and men. He mediates better than Moses, bringing men to God and God to men; for a master is better and greater than a servant. Moses was a servant, but Christ, as God, is Master. So “like me” refers to the clothing and the mediation. And Moses also said that whoever will not listen to that prophet shall have his soul cut off from among his people; and that he is the one who redeems Israel, the Lord who became man and lived among us men, and no other. Jeremiah said this earlier: “This is our God; no other shall be compared with him,” and so on. And the prophet Isaiah says: “Not an angel, not an envoy, but the Lord himself will come and save [?]

…the Jews because of your unbelief. The prophet Hosea says: “I will call those who were not my people ‘my people,’” that is, the nations that believed in him. And David, showing that God was going to become flesh for the sake of the nations, said: “God has become king over the nations.” Why did he not say, “He has become king over the Jews”? That God is king over all was plain; but before the nations believed, they did not know him as king, because they were held fast by idolatry and ruled tyrannically by demons. Through his dispensation in the flesh, however, he freed us from idols by his own blood, which he poured out on the cross, and became king over us, because we believed in him. That is why he says again: “All the nations you have made will come and worship before you, O Lord,” meaning all who come to him in this present age through holy baptism, as the same prophet urged us: “Come to him and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be put to shame.” And another prophet says: “Wash yourselves, be clean, remove the wickedness from your hearts.” If they come to him in this way, they will receive the reward of faith: to be saved through faith, without the worship of the law. But those who refuse to come to him now will, in the age to come, worship him even against their will, with great shame and much fear and trembling. As the prophet said: “Lord, your arm is lifted high, and they did not fear” (that is, now they have disbelieved), “but when they know, let them be put to shame” (that is, in the age to come they will know the Christ in whom they now disbelieve, and will be put to shame, and will be sent by him into the unquenchable fire to be punished forever). That Christ was to be manifested from Zion, and that he is the Most High and himself founded Zion, David said: “‘Mother Zion,’ a man will say, and a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her.” That he was to be baptized in the Jordan and receive testimony from above from God the Father, he said: “The voice of the Lord is upon the waters; the God of glory has thundered; the Lord is upon many waters.” That through holy baptism he crushed the devil and his powers, he says: “There you crushed the heads of the dragons upon the water,” that is, of the demons; “you shattered the head of the dragon,” that is, of the devil. That Christ himself is the maker of heaven and earth and sea, that he walked on the sea as on dry ground, that he performed many healings among the people, and that he was to suffer for the world, the book of Job says: “He who alone stretched out the heaven, who walks on the sea as on dry ground.” And the prophet says: “Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the tongue of the stammerers will speak clearly; then the

lame will leap like a deer.” That our Lord Jesus Christ was to come to Jerusalem to suffer, seated on the colt of a donkey, a beast of burden, arriving as king, the prophet Zechariah says: “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; proclaim it, daughter of Jerusalem: behold, your king is coming, righteous and bringing salvation, gentle and riding on a beast of burden and a colt.” That he was also hailed with “Hosanna” by your own children, the children of the Jews, who were taught this by God, David announced beforehand: “Out of the mouths of infants and nursing babies you have perfected praise.” And Isaiah says: “He took up our infirmities and bore our diseases, and he suffers pain for us.” Do you not see, O Jew, how the Scriptures of the prophets had to be fulfilled in him? Concerning his betrayal by Judas, one of his disciples, the Psalm says: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples plot new things? The kings of the earth stood ready, and the rulers gathered together.” For truly there gathered together against God’s holy Servant Jesus, who is the Christ, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the nations and the peoples of Israel. And David says about him: “They dug my hands and my feet; they divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots; they counted all my bones.” There is the crucifixion too. And that they gave him vinegar with gall to drink, the same David said again: “They gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.” Did the prophets lie, then, and the evangelists of us Christians, when they said the same things, that Christ suffered all this? If our evangelists lied, then the prophets lied too, since they said things just like these. Do you want to hear about his burial as well? The Prophet says in the book of Psalms: “They laid me in the lowest pit, in dark places and in the shadow of death, and I became like a man without help, free among the dead,” that is, sinless. And in Job it says: “The gates of death open to you in fear, and the gatekeepers of Hades cowered when they saw you,” meaning, of course, the powers of the hostile demons in Hades. That Christ, while hanging on the cross, raised from the dead many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep long ago, the Psalmist said: “He who leads out the prisoners with might; likewise those who embitter him, who dwell in tombs.” Zech. 9:9. Ps. 8:5. Job 38:17.

[?] and saw corruption; for God himself raised up the human nature which he had assumed. And elsewhere it is written: “And his rest shall be honor,” that is, the rest is his burial and the honor his resurrection. So who, hearing these things from the prophets about Christ, does not confess him to be true God, who became man for the salvation of the world, abolished idols and overthrew the sacrifices of demons? Where are the sacrifices of Egypt? Where are the oracles of Memphis? Where is Sebennytos, which worshipped Simon? Where is Nouphis, which worshipped wine? Where today are those who worshipped the sun? Where is the temple of Artemis? Where are the oracles of Apollo at the temple of Cyzicus, and of all the demons? Since Christ appeared and the cross was planted, God is worshipped and glorified everywhere. And are you not ashamed, you Jews, to call us idol-sacrificers and idolaters? Yet there is nothing strange in it: every harlot pins her own name on the free woman and shouts at her, “Harlot!” You did not spare Isaiah and Jeremiah and the rest of the prophets, nor even Christ himself; how could you spare us Christians? If you had the power that we have today, you would not let a single one of us live among you, as we put up with you. And since you have asked, “Why did the prophets not speak about Christ openly and plainly?” I in turn ask you this: Why did the prophets not tell you Jews about Christ, “Watch out, a man called Jesus is going to come; do not believe him, for he is a deceiver”? As it is, refusing to believe the true Christ and God whom the prophets proclaimed beforehand, you will accept a deceiver and not the Christ. If the Jew says, “God commanded us not to worship wood or stone or the works of men’s hands; how is it, then, that you Christians venerate and revere these things, making crosses and icons out of them?” say to him: “Tell me, Jew, why do you yourself venerate the book of the law, when it is made of skins tanned in uncleanness? And why did the patriarch Jacob bow down upon the top of Joseph’s staff?” And if he answers, “Even when I venerate the book of the law, I do not venerate the substance of the skins but the power of the words; and when Jacob bowed down to the staff, he did not worship the wood but Joseph who held it,” say to him: “In the same way we Christians, when we venerate the cross of Christ, do not worship the substance of the wood (God forbid!) but Christ who was crucified on it. And just as you, if you were to find now the two tablets and the two golden cherubim that Moses made, and the ark, would venerate them in honor of the one who commanded them to be made, so we too, when we venerate icons, do not worship the wood (God forbid!) but honor Christ and his saints. We worship neither the wood nor the painting, since we often wipe clean the

icons that have grown old and renew them, or burn them when they have rotted and make new ones, solely as a good reminder.” But you, tell me this: why did you worship the image of Nebuchadnezzar in Babylon, even though you had Daniel and other prophets there to teach you? When I, a Christian, venerate an icon of Christ, I say, “Glory to you, O God of the saints”; I do not say, “Glory to wood or painting.” But you, when you worshipped the image, said, “Glory to Nebuchadnezzar.” I venerate the cross and do not say, “Glory to wood” (God forbid!); but you worship the calf and say, “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” We Christians, though held captive for many years and oppressed, do not deny God. And if some Christians have denied him, there were not as many as there were of you in Babylon, when without being beaten or flogged, at a mere word, you all denied him and worshipped the image of a man. If the three youths had not kept faith with God, where, tell me, would you have kept faith with God? And this after seeing so many signs everywhere: in Egypt through Moses, at the Red Sea, in the wilderness, in the pillar of fire, in the cloud of light, on Mount Sinai. When did God ever do such good things for anyone? When did God ever speak to anyone like this, with laws and angelic trumpets and such signs: giving you the law, raining down manna, sending prophets among you, subduing the nations, destroying foreigners, handing over the tablets, designing your tabernacle himself, and appointing Moses over you as a second god, a figure of himself? O your great hardness of heart! O your evil mind! O your ungrateful choice and willful blindness! Up on the mountain Moses was contending for you, and down below you were casting the calf; up there he was entreating God, and down below you were provoking God and worshipping the calf. You ate the manna and reviled God. For David says: “While the food was still in their mouths, the wrath of God came up against them.” And what can you say against us Christians because we worship the Son of God? Tell me instead why you sacrificed your sons and daughters to demons, to Baal-Peor, as David says. What then? Do you have any faith at all? God forbid! Listen to Moses speaking to the people (and the Hebrew people was devout at that time), but listen to what Moses says: “For they are a perverse generation; there is no faith in them.” And again: “A crooked and perverse generation, is this how you repay the Lord?” And there are countless other damning testimonies about you in your prophecies, spoken by God: “I have begotten sons and raised them up,” he says, “but they have rejected me. The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger, but Israel has not known me, and my people has not understood. Woe, sinful nation, people full of sins!” And again the same prophet Isaiah says to you: “Hear

the word of the Lord, house of Sodom; give heed to the law of God, people of Gomorrah.” Do you see that God calls the Jews Sodomites, faithless, a foolish people, idol-sacrificers, ungrateful, an evil and perverse generation, and blemished children? “They sacrificed to demons and not to God; they forsook God who made them and turned away from God their Savior.” So let us search the Scriptures and see whether God has declared so much against any other nation. In Jerusalem you spent fifty-two years sacrificing to idols in the temple of God under your king Manasseh, profaning the temple and the city of God. For this reason God handed you over [?] twice to the Chaldeans into captivity in Babylon; then after seventy years he called you back again. Now this is what I want to learn from you. After you came up from Babylon and your temple was built a second time in Jerusalem, and you worshipped God in it and no longer sacrificed to idols, what sin did you commit before God, that for eight hundred years and more God has scattered you over all the earth? He brought Titus and Vespasian from Rome, and they slaughtered as many as a million of you in Jerusalem, as Josephus, your own historian, says (he alone records these things). They burned your temple, laid waste the altar and the holy places, the whole city and Zion, and took you captive; and you are scattered over all the earth, transgressing the law, to this day. For eight hundred years and more, as we said, you have kept no altar, no ark, no place for the Passover. For God told you: “You shall keep the Passover nowhere but in Jerusalem,” and not to go into Egypt. Your fathers sinned, and when they had been taken captive to Babylon a second time and the temple had been laid waste a second time, they obtained [?] God’s reconciliation with them and the rebuilding of the temple. But what sin did you commit, and so great a one, that God no longer raised up the temple for you and no longer brought you back from your enemies? Did you sacrifice your sons and daughters to idols as your fathers did? Did you worship an image as they did? Not at all. Did you set up an idol in the temple, as Manasseh did? Did you kill prophets? Not at all. Why, then, were you so forsaken by God? Truly, even if you do not say it, the stones will cry out: from the moment you crucified Christ you were forsaken. That is why, until now and forever, you have been forsaken, scattered, stripped bare, and cast out of the temple and of Zion. Your fathers, who made the calf, who broke the law in many ways, who worshipped the golden image and sacrificed their sons and daughters to the devil, were chastised for seventy years, and a hundred, in Babylon of Persia, and then called back. But you, who sinned against Christ, have been cast out not for seventy or a hundred years only, but until the end of the age. And we, the nations, have been called children of Christ; we serve him and glorify him, together with the Father and his Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

THIRD QUESTION BY THE SAME AUTHOR. Tell me, you Jews: the anointed one you are waiting for, what is he going to be? A Jew, then, who follows [?] … and who breaks the law and abolishes the sacrifices? … [?] … the law, renewing the sacrifices for our race? And tell me: how many years is it since the first captivity of the Jews under Nebuchadnezzar the Persian? They can answer, “A thousand years and more,” and that is so. Then say to them: “Look at what you have said. You say that your Christ who is coming is a Jew, that he will renew and offer the sacrifices of Moses, and that he has not yet come. You also say that from the time of Nebuchadnezzar, when Daniel was in Babylon, it has been a thousand years or more. On that last point you have spoken the truth. Now listen carefully. If, as you say, the coming Christ is a Jew, and he will perform the sacrifices of the law, and he has not yet come, then how does the prophet Daniel say in his visions what the archangel Gabriel taught him? Gabriel said: ‘Until Christ the leader, seventy weeks of years have been decreed for your people and for the holy city, to bring sin to an end.’ And a little later: ‘And to seal up vision and prophets, and to anoint the holy of holies, to abolish the sacrifice and the libation of the law.’ So show us now which Christ came, anointed as holy of holies, after the seventy weeks, that is, four hundred and ninety years after Daniel, and abolished the sacrifice and the libation of the law. When were the libation and the sacrifice of the law taken away? If you are not lying when you say that Christ has not yet come but is still to come, show us which Christ came as holy of holies four hundred and ninety years after Daniel. But you cannot point to anyone else who did this except Jesus Christ, the Son of God.
