And again, if you are telling the truth when you say that the coming Christ, our God, will offer the sacrifices of the law, then Daniel is lying when he says that ‘when Christ comes, sacrifice and libation will be taken away.’ And if we really are breaking the law by holding to the new covenant of Christ, and your coming Christ is going to renew the old covenant and the law of Moses, as you say, then where are we to look for that covenant which God spoke of through Jeremiah:

‘not like the covenant that I made with their fathers when I brought them out of the land of Egypt’? For after the law had been given to them, God said through the prophets Isaiah and Micah: ‘For out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.’ So when Christ came, he himself brought the new law and fulfilled the old.

The Jew: You Christians put your hope in a man who was hanged on a gallows and condemned.

The Christian: Which is more honoured before God, a man or a bronze serpent? Yet you venerate the serpent as it hangs. But listen with understanding. Tell me: did your fathers crucify someone called Jesus Christ, yes or no? And for what reason did you crucify him? “Because he was a lawbreaker and was destroying the law and the Sabbath.” Then of whom did the prophets proclaim that he would come in the last days? They said he would be sold, and for how much he would be sold. They said he would be led to death and nailed to the wood with nails through his hands and feet, that he would taste vinegar and gall, that he would be pierced with a spear, and that the sky would be darkened. And the words of the prophets could not fail to be fulfilled. What do you say to these things [?]? Were they fulfilled in our Christ, or are they still to happen to your anointed one? If they are still to happen to your anointed one, then look: you too put your hope in a condemned man. But if they were all fulfilled in our Christ, then agree with us and speak the truth. And if they refer neither to our Christ nor to your anointed one, then the prophets are simply lying. But perhaps, under pressure, you will admit against your will that your fathers killed our Christ by a shameful death, as a criminal and a destroyer of the law. In that case let us bring forward the prophets and see whether they call the one you crucified a criminal. But tell me, who on earth is without sin? As Scripture says, “No one is clean of filth, not even if his life lasts a single day.” Clearly no one is sinless except God alone. So let us hear what Isaiah says about our Christ who suffered: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer. Because of the iniquities of my people he was led to death. And I will give the wicked in return for his burial, and the rich in return for his death, for he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth.” Are you not ashamed, then? You have plainly disgraced yourselves. You said that you crucified him because he broke the law, but the prophet says that he committed no sin. And since no one is sinless except God alone, it is clear that the one you crucified is also true God, for he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth. Now let us see what the other prophets say about our Christ who suffered, whether they acknowledge him as a criminal or as Lord. For perhaps the sheer number of the prophets will put you to shame, and you will be silenced and stop speaking against Christ and the

Christians. See how Zechariah and Jeremiah the prophets speak in the same way about the selling of Christ and the thirty pieces of silver paid for him: “And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of the one who was valued, whom they valued from the sons of Israel, and they gave them for the potter’s field, as a burial place for strangers.” And the psalm shows that the Jews gave false testimony against him at the time of his passion: “Unjust witnesses rose up against me; they questioned me about things I did not know; they repaid me evil for good.” And the prophet shows that he endured these sufferings willingly, not against his will: “I gave my back to the whips and my cheeks to blows. I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting, and they spat on me with their filthy spittle.” Jeremiah speaks of his wearing a crown of thorns: “With the thorns of their iniquities they crowned me.” He was lifted up on the cross, and he carried on his own shoulders the beginning of our salvation, that is, the cross. Of this Isaiah says: “A child has been born to us, a son has been given to us, whose government is upon his shoulder.” That government is the cross. David shows that Christ was God and King before the ages, and that he was to be crucified in the midst of the earth for the salvation of his world: “But God, our King before the ages, has worked salvation in the midst of the earth.” And Zechariah likewise shows that they nailed his hands and feet: “Their wounds are between my hands. And he will say: These are the wounds I received in the house of my beloved.” See how, even after these sufferings, he calls you beloved, and still you do not turn to him. You are truly ungrateful. After he had died, his holy side was pierced with a spear, and blood and water gushed from it. Of this the prophet Zechariah said: “They will look on me, whom they pierced.” And Moses clearly prefigures this by the rock of flint, which he struck with his rod, and water gushed out for the salvation of the people. That rock was a figure of Christ. The rock of flint was lifeless and without feeling, yet when Moses’ rod struck it, at once it poured out water to give the people of that time a life that would pass away. In the same way the spotless body of Christ God, after it had died, at once poured out blood and water from his holy side for the salvation of those who believe in him, to give them a life that does not pass away but is eternal. And again the same prophet Moses speaks of the crucifixion of Christ and of your unbelief: “You will see your life hanging, and you will not believe.” See, he too calls the one who hung on the wood eternal life. And do not say that he said this about the bronze serpent. They did believe in the serpent. It was about the Life, that is, Christ, that he said, “You will not believe.” For Christ himself took on the curse that we brought upon ourselves through transgression and disobedience, as it is written: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.” The sinless one became a curse for

us, so that he might free us from the curse and grant eternal life to those who believe in him. For you Jews believed in the bronze serpent hanging on the wood, even though the serpent was cursed above every beast. It held out an image to your forefathers. Just as the serpent that did not bite brought life against the serpents that bit, so too Christ, who was sinless, was hung up for sinners and granted life to the world. On the day Christ was crucified, the day was darkened. He gave a loud cry when he breathed his last, and heaven and the whole earth were shaken because of this outrage committed by the Jews. Of this the prophet Hosea says: “The sun and the moon will be darkened, and the stars will withhold their light. The Lord will roar from Zion, and heaven and earth will be shaken.” And David says: “The Most High uttered his voice; the earth was shaken.” See, they too call the crucified one Lord Most High. And Zechariah the prophet says: “And the Lord God will come, and all the saints with him. On that day there will be no light. It will be neither day nor night, and toward evening there will be light, and that day is known to the Lord.” For from the sixth hour until the ninth hour there was darkness over all the earth. See, Zechariah too has called the crucified one Lord and God. Perhaps you will say that these passages speak of your anointed one. Then look: you too put your hope in a man who is going to be crucified as a condemned criminal. But the one prophesied is no other than our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God. He came down from heaven and became flesh of the Holy Spirit and of the ever-virgin Mary, and he suffered these things for the salvation of the world, just as the prophets foretold about him. We have set out their testimonies and prophecies about Christ in our discussion. And about his being taken up into heaven and sitting at the right hand of God, Zechariah also said: “On that day the feet of the Lord shall stand on the Mount of Olives, which faces Jerusalem on the east.” And the Psalmist says: “He mounted upon the cherubim and flew upon the wings of the winds,” and “God has gone up with a shout,” and “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand,” and the rest. What does “he went up” mean, except that he had first come down? Yet besides everything we have said, we bring before you not only prophets but other witnesses as well, people who followed closely the coming of Christ in the flesh. What we are about to say, you also have in your records. At that time your fathers were utterly defeated, and they tried to turn their defeat into an unbeatable victory. So they ordered that no Jew should keep any written account of what Christ had done, or search for such accounts or read them at all. They did not want anyone’s diligent study to give the many knowledge of these things. But you know these things,

and we are telling them to you even though habit forces you to hide the truth. Did you not hear of the Magi who crossed from Persia into Palestine? They were guided by a divine oracle and led by a star, and they worshipped Christ and offered him gifts. After this your high priests of that time met with Herod, who was king then, and he asked them, “Where is the Christ to be born?” They told him, “In Bethlehem, the city of Judea, as the prophets say.” Herod was jealous of the kingdom that had sprung up, and so he carried out that great slaughter of children. Is not John the Baptist descended from the Jews? Your fathers sent to him at that time to ask whether he was the Christ. He said, “I am not.” Instead he pointed out the Christ to them and said, “This is the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.” And then there are the others. Nicodemus your ruler, Nathanael, Joseph of Arimathea, Bizes [?] and Alexander, who also ate with him at the wedding of Simon the Galilean, where he turned the water into wine. The elders whom the centurion sent to plead for his servant, to trouble Jesus for the servant’s healing: “For he is worthy,” they said, “that you should grant him this, for he loves our nation, and he himself built our synagogue for us.” The royal official, the proconsul [?], the brother of Jairus the ruler of the synagogue, whose son he made well. This man’s brother Jairus, who pleaded with him and whose daughter he raised from the dead. Caiaphas, your high priest that year, who advised that one man should die rather than the whole nation perish. Your children, who then cried out, “Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel!” Judas the disciple, who agreed to take thirty pieces of silver to hand him over to you. The soldiers to whom you gave the silver so that they would say, “His disciples came by night and stole him while we were asleep.” Josephus your historian, who spoke about Christ and called him a righteous and good man, revealed by divine grace, who did good to many through signs and wonders. Whose garments did they divide, as the prophet says, casting lots for them? Whose hands and feet did they pierce? To whom did they give vinegar and gall to drink when he was thirsty, hanging on the cross? About whom did Moses say, “You will see your life hanging before your eyes, and you will not believe”? If you believed Moses, you would believe Christ too. But your fathers would not obey Moses. They pushed him aside and turned back to Egypt in their hearts, and said to Aaron, “Make us gods to go before us, for as for this Moses who brought us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.” In those days they made a calf, offered sacrifice to the idol and rejoiced in the works of their hands. But God turned away and handed them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the

prophets: “Did you offer me slain victims and sacrifices for forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel? You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the images you made in order to worship them”; “and I will remove you beyond Babylon.” Your fathers had the tent of witness in the wilderness, just as the one who spoke to Moses commanded him to make it, according to the pattern he had seen. Your fathers in turn received it and brought it in with Joshua when they took possession of the land of the nations that God drove out before them. It remained until the days of David, who found favour before God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. But it was Solomon who built a house for him. Yet the Most High does not dwell in temples made with hands, as the prophet says: “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool for my feet. What house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest? Did not my hand make all these things?” O Jews, stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did. They killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One. Did not your fathers in Jerusalem become murderers and betrayers? In the same way you too, their children, imitate them. You do not believe the words of the prophets and you go on hating Christ, you who received the law as delivered by angels and did not keep it. And the Holy Spirit says through the mouth of David the prophet: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion, on the day of testing in the wilderness, where your fathers tested me and tried me and saw my works. For forty years I was angry with that generation, and I said: They always go astray in their heart; they have not known my ways. So I swore in my anger: They shall not enter my rest.” But not all who came out of Egypt entered [?], for those who disobeyed and disbelieved provoked him. With whom was he angry for forty years, if not with those who sinned and disobeyed, whose bodies fell in the wilderness? And to whom did he swear that they would not enter his rest, if not to those who disobeyed? And we see that they could not enter because of their unbelief, except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun. Six hundred [thousand?] perished [?], for he said that these thousands had come out of Egypt. When God commanded them to set out for the promised land, they refused, pleading their fear and the great size of the enemy. For this reason the God of all destroyed them all, one by one, in the wilderness, and brought in their children in their place, that is, those with Caleb son of Jephunneh, and Joshua son of Nun gave them rest. And suppose David the prophet spoke of rest in the land itself, since that was where Joshua gave them
rest. Yet the divine David was living in that land when he said these words and promised the rest: “Today, if you hear his voice,” and the rest.

So there still remains another Sabbath rest and another rest, which is faith in Christ, as the Lord says through Jeremiah the prophet: “Behold, the days are coming when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah.” By saying “new,” he has made the first one old. “Not like the covenant I made with their fathers on the day I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt. For they did not remain faithful to my covenant, and so I disregarded them, says the Lord. For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel: I will put my laws into their minds, and I will write them on their hearts. I will be their God, and they shall be my people.” So then, faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God. One must first hear, and then receive the words of God in mind and heart and believe, just as “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.” “For by works of the law no flesh will be justified.” “For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse, for it is written: Cursed is everyone who does not abide by all the things written in the book of the law, and do them.” It is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for “the righteous shall live by faith” in them [?]. Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness. And Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the nations by faith, proclaimed the gospel in advance to

Know, then, that it is those who have faith who are the sons of Abraham. The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. It does not say “in your seeds,” as if referring to many, but refers to one: “in your seed.” For this is a covenant ratified beforehand by God in Christ. The law, which came four hundred and thirty years afterward, does not annul it and make the promise void. The old Scripture too calls the promise made to Abraham a covenant of God. The God of all promised to bless the nations through the seed of Abraham, and this seed is Christ the Master himself, for through him the promise was fulfilled. For if the inheritance comes from the law, it no longer comes from the promise. But God gave the seed to Abraham freely, through a promise. Why, then, the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the seed to whom the promise had been made should come. The law was established to take care of the race from which that seed was to spring according to the flesh. It was established with angels assisting, and Moses served in giving it. But if you call yourself a Jew and rely on the law, so that you boast in the law, then by breaking the law you dishonour God

[?]: "Circumcision indeed is of value if you keep the law; but if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision," as Jeremiah says: "All the nations are uncircumcised in the flesh, but the house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart." "Be circumcised to God, and circumcise the foreskin of your heart." "For through the law comes knowledge of sin. But now the righteousness of God has been made manifest, attested by the law and the prophets: the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ, for all and upon all who believe. We are justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus." "We reckon, then, that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law." What then? "Is God the God of the Jews only? Is he not of the Gentiles also? Yes, of the Gentiles also, since God is one, who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith. Do we then make the law void through faith? By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law." "For what does the Scripture say? Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness." "For David says: Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not reckon sin." "The law," he says, "brings punishment on those who sin, but the prophet calls blessed those who have received forgiveness of their sins." Is this blessing, then, for the circumcised or for the uncircumcised? We say that faith was reckoned to Abraham as righteousness. How, then, was it reckoned? When he was circumcised, or when he was uncircumcised? Clearly not when he was circumcised, but when he was uncircumcised. And he received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness of the faith that he had while uncircumcised, so that he might be the father of all who believe while uncircumcised, so that righteousness might be reckoned to them as well; and the father of circumcision, not to those of the circumcision only, but also to those who walk in the footsteps of the faith that your father Abraham had while uncircumcised. For the promise to Abraham or to his seed, that he should be heir of the world, did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith. For the law brings about wrath (since it is the law's way to punish those who transgress it); for where there is no law, neither is there transgression. That is why it is of faith, so that it may be by grace, in order that the promise may be secure for all the seed: not only for those of the law, but also for those of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all, as it is written, "I have made you the father of many nations." He stood before God, in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and speaks of things that are not as though they were. Against hope he believed in hope, that he might become the father of many nations, according to what had been said: "So shall your seed be." And not weakening in faith, he did not consider his own body, already as good as dead, since he was about a hundred years old, nor the deadness of Sarah's womb; and with regard to the promise of God he did not

waver in unbelief, but grew strong in faith, giving glory to God, fully convinced that what he had promised he was able also to do. That is why it was also reckoned to him as righteousness. "Now it was not written for his sake alone that it was reckoned to him as righteousness, but for ours also, to whom it is going to be reckoned, to us who believe in him who raised our Lord Jesus Christ from the dead." "For not all who are of Israel are Abraham's seed"; rather, [?] seeks the kinship of virtue. "Nor are they all children of God because they are Abraham's seed; but 'In Isaac shall your seed be called'; that is, it is not the children of the flesh who are children of God, but the children of the promise are reckoned as seed." He calls "children of the flesh" [?] those born according to the ordinary course of nature, and "children of the promise" those granted by grace through faith. For this is the word of promise: "At this season I will come, and Sarah shall have a son." When nature had given up, he was shown to be a father by divine generosity. Why then are you so proud, O Jew, as though you alone were called Abraham's seed? Ishmael too was Abraham's son, and his firstborn. And if you think he was excluded from the kinship as being half-slave, yet it is the custom of Scripture to trace descent through fathers and not through mothers. And those born of Keturah, who was a free woman, are nevertheless not called Abraham's seed. Consider also the twelve sons of Jacob, born of different mothers, four of them half-slave, yet all of them bearing the name of Israel and in no way harmed by their mothers' slavery. And not only these, but also Rebecca, when she had conceived by one man, our father Isaac: "For though the children were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad (so that God's purpose according to election might stand, not by works but by him who calls), it was said to her: The elder shall serve the younger." Or do you think, O Jew, that it was because of Sarah that Isaac was preferred over Ishmael and over the sons born to Abraham of Keturah? What would you say, then, about Rebecca? For here there was one mother and one conception, since the children were twins; this is what "having conceived by one" means: she conceived both at the same time. Yet the one was beloved of God, and the other unworthy of divine care. God did not wait to test them by their deeds, but proclaimed the difference between them in advance, from the children still in the womb; and he proclaimed it in advance because he foresaw the purpose of each. For the election is not unjust, but corresponds to the purpose of the men themselves, as it is written: "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated." The saying spoken by God to Abraham, "In Isaac shall your seed be called," shows that not the whole of the race shared in the blessing. For God does not look to nature, but seeks faith and virtue, as he also says in Hosea: "I will call

those who were Not my people 'My people,' and her who was Not beloved 'Beloved'; and in the place where it was said to them, 'You are not my people,' there they shall be called sons of the living God." "For the Gentiles, who did not know righteousness, attained righteousness"; and by righteousness he means the righteousness that comes from faith. "But Israel, pursuing a law of its own righteousness, did not attain righteousness. Why? Because they pursued it not by faith but by works of the law." For they thought that a way of life lived according to the law was enough for them to acquire righteousness, and they despised faith; and for that reason they had no share in the gifts of faith either. "For they stumbled over the stone of stumbling, as it is written: Behold, I lay in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence, and everyone who believes in him shall not be put to shame." Those who take the meaning of the prophetic Scriptures in another direction, and are unwilling to advance along the road, are prone to stumble. This is what happened to the Jews: being occupied with the superfluities of the law, they were unwilling to see the stone spoken of by the prophets, although the prophets clearly foretold that whoever believes in it will obtain the greatest of blessings. "For they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God and seeking to establish their own righteousness, they did not submit to the righteousness of God." "For Christ is the end of the law, for righteousness to everyone who believes." For the law guided us all, that is, the whole of human nature, to Christ the Master. So whoever believes in Christ the Savior fulfills the aim of the law. For it stands in Scripture: "Behold, I lay in Zion a cornerstone, chosen and precious, and whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame." "To us who believe, then, belongs the honour; but for those who disobey, 'The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner,' and 'a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence.' They stumble at the Word because they disobey, as they were also destined to do." But we who believe and have been baptized are "a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, so that we may proclaim the excellencies of him who called us out of darkness into his marvellous light. Once we were not a people, but now we are the people of God; once we had not received mercy, but now we have received mercy." "Us he also called, not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles, as he also says in Hosea: I will call those who were Not my people 'My people,' and her who was Not beloved 'Beloved'; and in the place where it was said to them, 'You are not my people,' there they shall be called sons of the living God." "For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God." "For Christ is the end of the law, for righteousness to everyone who believes." "For Moses writes of the righteousness that comes from the law, that the man who does these things shall live by them. But the righteousness that comes from faith speaks thus: Do not say in your heart, 'Who will ascend into heaven?' (that is, to bring Christ down), or, 'Who will descend into the abyss?' (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). But what does it say? The word is near you, in your mouth

and in your heart (that is, the word of faith that we preach): that if you confess with your mouth Jesus Christ as Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth one confesses unto salvation. For the Scripture says, 'Whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame.' For the same Lord is Lord of all, rich toward all who call on him; and everyone who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved. How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without someone preaching? And how shall they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of good things! Indeed, their voice has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world." "But did Israel not know? Isaiah says: Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?" "And Moses first says: I will make you jealous of those who are no nation; with a senseless nation I will provoke you to anger." He called us senseless nations, for before faith we showed foolishness: we were once, that is, before we believed, foolish, disobedient, led astray. God grieved the Jews in a special way, that is, he pained them; for the dispersion and the desolation of the temple were not as painful as the piety and renown of the Gentiles. "And Isaiah is very bold and says: I was found by those who did not seek me; I became manifest to those who did not ask for me." In this very passage he showed both the foretelling of the Gentiles' knowledge of God and the bloodthirstiness of the Jews. For this is what "is very bold" indicates: he was not afraid, it says, of the murderous and raging Jews, but with great boldness proclaimed in advance the salvation of the Gentiles. He also foretold the unbelief of the Jews, as what follows shows: "But to Israel Moses says: All day long I have stretched out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people." In this way the wonderful prophets both accuse the Jews and proclaim in advance the faith of the Gentiles. "Now I say that our Lord Jesus Christ became a servant to the circumcised for the sake of God's truth, in order to confirm the promises made to the fathers, and that the Gentiles will glorify God for his mercy." For the God of all promised Abraham that he would bless the nations in his seed, and the patriarch himself and all his race received the sign of circumcision. It was therefore fitting that his seed according to the flesh, from which the blessing would flow out to the nations, should also bear the sign of kinship, so that the truth of the divine promise might be clearly shown. And the nations, having received grace, will praise the giver of loving-kindness, who through his divine prophets foretold the faith and salvation of the nations, as it is written: "Therefore

we will confess you among the nations, O Lord, and sing to your name." And again it says: "Praise the Lord, all you nations, and extol him, all you peoples." And again Isaiah says: "There shall be the root of Jesse, he who rises to rule the nations; in him the nations will hope." As it is written: "Those to whom nothing was announced concerning him will see, and those who have not heard will understand." "And when he again brings the firstborn into the world, he says: Let all the angels of God worship him." So also God says through the mouth of the blessed David: "Once for all I have sworn by my holiness; I will not lie to David. His seed shall endure forever, and his throne like the sun before me, and like the moon established forever, and the witness in heaven [?]." And again: "I will set his hand upon the sea, and his right hand upon the rivers. He will call upon me: You are my Father, my God, and the helper of my salvation. And I will make him the firstborn, high [?] among the kings of the earth." He is the Word of God and only-begotten Son, Maker of the ages and Creator of all things. From where, then, does he enter the world? And how is the Only-begotten firstborn? How? Through the dispensation of his incarnation. And if the angels worshipped him after the incarnation, did they not by all means offer him this honour before the incarnation as well? God was everywhere, and he entered the world as man: "He was in the world, and the world came into being through him, and the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him." For if he was in the world, how did he come? And if he came, how was he in the world? Rather, he was in the world as God, and came as man. He is Only-begotten as God, and firstborn among many brothers as man. He always received veneration from the angels, for he was always God; but they also worshipped him as man. "And of the angels he says: 'He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire'; but of the Son: 'Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the sceptre of uprightness is the sceptre of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated lawlessness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.'" By this he clearly showed that the angels have a created nature, but that the nature of the only-begotten Son is uncreated and eternal. For as God he has an eternal throne, a kingdom without beginning and without end. But "You have loved righteousness and hated lawlessness," and what follows, is said with respect to his humanity. For the prophet Isaiah too, after foretelling the things concerning Emmanuel, added this as well: "Before the child knows good or evil, he refuses wickedness and chooses the good." And the anointing, too, is not of the Godhead,

but of the humanity; for it says, "with the oil of gladness above your companions." And we too are companions and partakers, not of the Godhead but of the humanity, as it is written: "For he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one." This too is said with respect to the humanity, for the nature that was assumed is created. Our Maker is indeed one [?], but we are sanctified through that nature, "for which reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying: I will proclaim your name to my brothers; in the midst of the assembly I will sing your praise. And again: I will put my trust in him. And again: Behold, I and the children whom God has given me." He who is Master and Maker of all took flesh for the salvation of his servants and became man of the holy Ever-Virgin, like us in every respect apart from sin. He ate and drank with his servants, condescended to them, healed their sick by his own power, and accepted the passion on our behalf; and so he is not ashamed to call brothers those for whom he endured the passion, that is, the faithful. And not only brothers, but also children: "Since therefore the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same, so that through his death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and set free all those who through fear of death were held in slavery all their lives." And how could he be called our brother, or truly call us children, if he did not wear the same nature? For this reason he took it up, destroyed the dominion of death, and dispelled the fear that lay upon us; for we go on living continually in fear of death. "For surely it is not angels that he takes hold of; he takes hold of the seed of Abraham." For if he had assumed the nature of angels, he would have been beyond the reach of death. But since the body he took was human, through the passion he paid the debt of mankind, and by rising in the body that had suffered he displayed his own power. "Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect." For like us he partook of food, endured hunger, was distressed and wept, and accepted death, "so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in the things that pertain to God, to make atonement for the sins of the people. For because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are afflicted." These things too are said with respect to his humanity. For he is not our high priest as God, but as man; nor did he suffer as God, but as man; nor did he learn our condition by experience, for as God and Creator he knows all things clearly. "To which of the angels has he ever said, 'Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet'?" For he does not say "Sit at my right hand" to him simply as God; otherwise how would his throne be forever and ever? It was as man, then, that he received a share in this honour; as God he has an eternal throne. And again: "What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you care for him? You made him

a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honour, and set him over the works of your hands; you subjected all things beneath his feet." "But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels because of the suffering of death, so that apart from God he might taste death for everyone, crowned with glory and honour." He was made lower than the angels not in the nature of his Godhead but in that of his humanity. Just as, then, he was lower than the angels as man because of the suffering of death (since the angels have an immortal nature, whereas he as man endured the passion apart from God for the [?] of all) [?] having [?] nature, it needed this treatment, the medicine of the incarnation; for the divine nature alone stands in need of nothing. This is what is meant by "apart from God he will taste death for everyone." And we see him crowned with glory and honour as man; for after the resurrection and the ascension into heaven he received a share in the divine glory and became superior to the angels. He sat down far above every principality and authority and power and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come. "For in subjecting all things to him, he left nothing that is not subject to him. But as it is, we do not yet see all things subjected to him." [?] will rule [?]; they will be subjected, for then even those who now oppose him will be subjected. For God the Word, having become man, destroyed the power of death, and having destroyed it, he promised us the resurrection. With the resurrection, incorruption and immortality are joined, and in it lies the endless rest promised through faith to our fathers, and eternal life for all who through a like faith hope in our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God. For if the perfect rest were in Jerusalem, Joshua the son of Nun would have brought us into it. But God did not give Abraham an inheritance in it, not even a foot's breadth, nor did he give an inheritance in it forever to his children who resemble him through faith. Rather, we dwell in it as sojourners and in everything pursue the passing things of this world. But there is the endless rest, which those who hear by faith today will inherit, in the words of the divine David, if they do not harden their hearts like the wicked fathers in the provocation on the day of testing. For just as those men did not enter the present, temporary rest because of unbelief, but their corpses fell in the wilderness, and their children entered it in their place, so those who have now heard the word of faith, and on receiving it have been enlightened, are to enter at the resurrection into the eternal rest promised by God through the mouth of David. But those who did not believe and who tempted God will be sent away into eternal fire, to be punished eternally. "Do not be ignorant of this, that your fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea

…passed through, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink; for they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.” These things, he says, were types of yours. The sea imitated the baptismal font, the cloud the grace of the Spirit, Moses the priest, the rod the cross, and Israel, passing through and crossing over, imitated those who are baptized. The pursuing Egyptians filled the role of a type of the demons, and Pharaoh himself was an image of the devil; for after the crossing the Israelites were set free from the domination of the Egyptians. And they received the manna from heaven as a kind of type of the heavenly bread, the body of Christ. The rock, too, imitated his side, for beyond all hope it at once gushed forth streams; and the rock was to them what Christ is to us. Yet it was not the rock that followed them, but the divine grace of Christ, the Son and Word of God, which also caused that rock, beyond all hope, to send forth streams of water. For if the rock followed them, or the rock's streams, how is it that they needed the divine grace again for water? “Men of Israel, and you who fear God, listen. God chose your fathers and exalted the people during their sojourn in the land of Egypt, and with an uplifted arm he led them out, and for about forty years he bore with their ways; he gave them their land as an inheritance. And after that, for about four hundred and fifty years, he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet. Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. And when he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, to whom he also bore witness and said, ‘I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my own heart, who will do all my will.’ From this man's offspring God, according to his promise, has brought salvation to Israel, after John had proclaimed before his coming a baptism of repentance to Israel. And as John was finishing his course, he said, ‘Who do you suppose that I am? I am not he. But behold, after me one is coming, the sandal of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.’ Men, brothers, sons of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, to you the word of this salvation has been sent. For those who live in Israel and their rulers, because they did not recognize him nor understand the voices of the prophets which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him. And though they found no cause for death, they asked Pilate to have him put to death. And when they had carried out everything written about him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb. But God raised him from the dead, and for many days he appeared to those who had come up [?] with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who have become his witnesses among the people and to

his disciples and apostles; appearing to them for forty days after his resurrection, he spoke with them about the kingdom of heaven. They also proclaimed to you, and likewise proclaim to us, the good news of the promise made to the fathers: that God has fulfilled it for their children by raising up Jesus for us, as it is also written in the psalm, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’ And that he raised him from the dead, never again to return to corruption, they have stated thus: ‘I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.’ Therefore he also says in another psalm, ‘You will not let your Holy One see corruption.’ For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers, and saw corruption; but he whom God raised up did not see corruption. Let it be known to you, therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is justified from all the things from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses. Beware, therefore, lest what is said in the prophets come upon you: ‘Look, you scoffers, and wonder, and perish; for I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe even if someone tells it to you.’” And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, only the remnant will be saved; for the Lord will carry out his word on the earth, cutting it short.” Thus the God of all foresaw from the beginning both those who would come to him by faith and those sick with unbelief. For since they say that only a few of them received the preaching, while all the rest, being deceived, fled from it, he showed that these things had been foretold from the beginning: even if they surpass in the multitude of their number and match the sand of the sea, not all will obtain salvation, but only those adorned with faith. For by the “word cut short” which the Lord will carry out he meant faith; and those who have come by faith are the ones called the remnant by the prophet, who will be saved through faith. “Or do you not know what the Scripture says of Elijah, how he pleads with God against Israel, saying, ‘Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have torn down your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life’? But what does the divine answer say to him? ‘I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.’” At that time, he says, Israel numbered many tens of thousands, and all were called Israelites; yet the God of all named himself God of the seven thousand and rejected all the others. The prophet, however, did not know even this, and thought that the remnant of true piety was preserved in himself alone. So it is nothing new or strange if you too are unaware of those of your people who have believed in the Savior, whom the God of all calls his people. “So too at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace.

And if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace.” Just as then, he says, out of countless tens of thousands only seven thousand were left free of impiety, so also now those who have disbelieved are more numerous than those who have enjoyed the divine grace. For it was not life according to the law that justified them (this is what “from works of the law” means), but the grace of God saved them. For this reason salvation is also called grace, since it came about through God's love for humankind, as it is written: “The Deliverer will come from Zion and will turn away ungodliness from Jacob; and this will be my covenant with them, when I take away their sins.” If life according to the law bestowed the forgiveness of their sins, the prophetic word would have foretold that; but since the law punishes sinners, and the Jews were always called lawless, it is plain that the prophetic word refers to the forgiveness bestowed through baptism. And he calls “Israel” all who believe, whether from the Gentiles or from the Jews, gathered to him by the nobility of faith. “What then? What Israel according to the flesh seeks, it did not obtain.” Why did it not obtain it? “Because it did not seek it by faith but by works of the law. The elect obtained it” through faith, “and the rest were hardened,” that is, were left to their unbelief, as it is written: “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear, [?] to this very day.” For God did not cause them to disbelieve; he allowed it, that is, he permitted it. By “spirit of stupor” he meant an unchangeable disposition: just as one who possesses praiseworthy compunction does not [?] a turn for the worse, so one who has given himself over entirely to wickedness does not choose a change for the better. And another prophet says: “For the heart of this people has grown dull, and with their ears they have heard with difficulty, and they have shut their eyes, and did not wish to see the light.” And David says: “Let their table become a snare and a trap and a stumbling block and a retribution for them; let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and bend their back continually [?]
The Jew asked: “Why do you Christians eat pork?” The Christian said: “Why do you not eat it?” The Jew: “Because it is unclean.” The Christian: “Then

why do you eat chicken, which is most unclean? It eats mice and snakes and every kind of filth. Yet you do not eat the swallow, which is cleaner than the chicken; nor the cuttlefish, which is clean and bloodless [?] and cleaner than the chicken, which eats even refuse [?] and carrion—but those you do not eat at all. Do you want to learn for what reason God told the Jews through Moses not to eat pork? It is because, while they were in Egypt with the Egyptians, they ate the pig, whereas the Egyptians worshipped the ox, the goat and the dog as gods. Hence some were called [?] because they worshipped the ox, and Cynites because they worshipped the dog. And so the Jews, living among them, took up their customs. When God, then, led them out of Egypt, wishing to turn their hearts away from the four-footed animals they had worshipped in Egypt, he commanded them to slaughter and eat here the very animals they had held sacred and worshipped there, so that by slaughtering and eating them they would no longer honor them. But the pig, which they used to eat in Egypt, he commanded them not to taste—not because it was unclean, but so that they would not turn back in their hearts to Egypt; and also so that, being forced not to eat it, they would lay hold of the other animals instead and slaughter and eat them—the ox, the goat, the sheep—which they had worshipped as gods while they were in Egypt. It was for this reason that the Jews were commanded by law not to eat pork, and not on account of uncleanness; for there are other things more unclean, as we have said, which are eaten even by the Jews. But God did not make these things unclean, or call them so; rather, he gave them to us as very good to eat, and granted that we have them also for other necessary uses. For apart from being slaughtered and eaten, the ox can also render us other use and service—plowing, transport and the rest—toiling with us at the other tasks of farming; the sheep gives its wool for our clothing; likewise the goat gives milk, cheese and hair; so too the dog is for guarding, the cat for clearing out vermin, the chicken for its eggs. But the pig has no other use except to be eaten, since it is unprofitable and useless on the land. You Jews make it unclean through your childishness, not wanting to buy it and raise it; for if you want to raise it, whatever the sheep and the goat eat is also the natural food of the pig. Hear the Scripture, which says: ‘And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good.’”
ANOTHER QUESTION. If a Hebrew says to you, “How are you, Christian, a child of Abraham, when you are a Gentile?” you will say to him: “By

faith, as was said to him: ‘I have made you the father of many nations.’ But you, Jew, how are you a child of Abraham? Question. If a Hebrew says to you, “How can you believe in the crucified one? If this is so, how can you still doubt the Godhead in three hypostases? How can you not worship the Son? How can you not believe in the Spirit? “But Scripture proclaims one God.” What need is there to say much? Leave Isaiah aside, pass over David and every other Scripture through which the life-giving Trinity is magnificently proclaimed; go up to Abraham's tent and consider carefully who they were who appeared to him, how many in number, and what and how many things the patriarch said to them. For to Abraham, who was perfect in knowledge, they appeared as three yet spoke as one, and so he too addressed them, saying: “Turn aside, Lord, to me.” What could be clearer [?] than this? What could express more vividly the Trinity of equal honor? By saying “Turn aside” in the plural he [?] the distinction of the persons, while by saying “Lord” in the singular he showed their one nature and lordship. But if you say that the one is God and the others angels, you are simply mad, and seem utterly ridiculous to me. For when have servants dared to sit down with their Master? Or when, at an appearance of God, have we heard of only two angels attending him as a guard? Clearly, then, it was the holy Trinity, equal in honor and sharing one throne, that was made known to Abraham. Why then, having heard this, do you rage against the truth again like a dog, saying: “If God is worshipped in Trinity, why was this not clearly made known to Israel by the prophets?” Hear, then: since Israel had long spent a great deal of time in Egypt and had learned the polytheistic religion of the Egyptians, God, who orders all things for our benefit, did not openly teach them the doctrines concerning the Trinity, lest Israel take from this a pretext for polytheism and return once more to the error of the Egyptians. For this reason he wisely and providentially veiled the mystery of the Trinity in every way. For if he had set forth the complete teaching from the very beginning, unruly Israel would surely have bolted and run back to its former ruin. For if, hearing nothing of the kind, it kept forgetting the one God hour by hour and was wholly attached to Egyptian impiety, what would it not have done had it been taught about the Trinity straight away? Because of the plurality, it would have thought it was seeing those very many gods that were worshipped in Egypt.

I have something else to say to you besides this. Since Christ, as you testify, said that he was a man and not God, why did you crucify him? Was it not for that? Then for what reason? “As a lawbreaker and one who violated the Sabbath.” And how, in what way, tell me? Because he made the paralytic walk on the Sabbath? Because he straightened the woman who was bent over? Because he raised a man four days dead? And what sort of lawbreaking is that? One who pulls a beast out of a pit on the Sabbath is not said to break the law, yet one who brought a stinking corpse back to life breaks it? O unjust judgment! O your madness! That among you beasts a beast should be judged better than a man! But why do you cling so tightly to the honor of the Sabbath, wretched and foolish man? Long ago God, while commanding that the Sabbath be honored and that you do no work on it, nevertheless, if an eight-day-old child happened to fall due on the Sabbath, had it circumcised without hindrance, thereby clearly showing that when the true eighth-day circumcision should one day come—which is the holy Lord's Day—the Sabbath would be abolished. For this day comes after the seventh, which is why it is also called the eighth. And it may very fittingly be called circumcision, for on it, when our Lord Jesus Christ rose from the dead, sin was cut away and the pride of the demons was brought low. What need is there to say much? Long ago God hinted at the abolition and change of the Sabbath, both through the eighth-day circumcision, as we have already said, and no less later through Jeremiah, when he promised to make a New Covenant. So do not be vexed, nor fight contentiously against us, if, along with everything else, the honor of the Sabbath too is transferred. For since the Covenant is new, its decrees too must be something new; and what is now set before us is surely new, not the same as what has passed, in reality and in appearance alike. And to show this the Lord said: “I will make a New Covenant, not like the covenant I made with your fathers when I led them out of Egypt.” If this is so, it is reasonable to expect the abolition of the Sabbath, the change of circumcision, and the change of many other legal ordinances. For if those old Mosaic decrees were to remain forever and stand firm to the end, he would not have said through Jeremiah that the old would pass away and other, new ones would come in their place. What this New Covenant is, and in what place it is given, Isaiah will teach you, saying: “Out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.” But see the wisdom of God: foreseeing your disobedience and unbelief, through the one prophet he gave notice of the New Covenant, and through the other he made known the very place in which this legislation was to be given. In vain, then, do you cling to the honor of the Sabbath; in vain do you hold fast to circumcision; for God, in granting a New Covenant, has abolished all these things. Besides, since circumcision was given as a sign

You are compelled to be circumcised in the flesh, but I am circumcised in the heart, so that I may not devise evil.” To show that this kind of circumcision is pleasing to God, hear what he says through Jeremiah when he accuses Israel: “All the nations are uncircumcised in the flesh, but the house of Israel is uncircumcised in their hearts.” Can circumcision of the foreskin justify anyone? Of Anastasius of Antioch, from the discourse On Energies. The coming together of the two natures produced one hypostasis. Human nature existed, that is, the common form from which our lump was assumed. It did not previously exist in a hypostasis of its own, but once assumed it is ascribed the same hypostasis as the one who assumed it. For just as the Word is united to the Father by nature, so he is also united to us. And in the respect in which the Word is distinct from the Father, namely by hypostasis, he is likewise distinct from us. For he is not of the same hypostasis with us as he is of the same nature with us, since he is not of the same hypostasis with his own Father either; nature and hypostasis are not the same thing. To himself, however, he is united by hypostasis, remaining that which he was before the ages, the Son. The union he has with himself he cannot have either with the Father or with us, for the union of the natures is hypostatic, and his hypostasis is one and the same. Being Son, he is still Son even after uniting human nature to himself. He did not take another hypostasis and unite it to himself; rather, he fitted a nature incorruptibly [?] to his own hypostasis. He is God and man in essence, but the same one in hypo[stasis…] [?] …they supposed to say of the Trinity. But if we always confess that it acts inseparably with the Word who is joined and co-subsists with it, and we do not say that it pre-existed its union with him…

…those who spout whatever they like without examining it slander us wickedly. We will show more clearly what we mean by an example. Suppose there are three bronze pillars, and one of them is heated to the extreme and has a rod placed in its hand. Then, because the other two do no harm to those who touch them, while this one cannot be touched because of the fierceness of the heat, are there for that reason four pillars and not three? Or did the bronze depart from its own nature when it was heated? Did it not rather take on the fire as an addition, and acquire the activity of its essence, operation and power [?]? Let us explain the point in another way too. Suppose again that there are three bronze statues, and that one is coated with wax, or kneaded over [?], or perhaps with gold or clay, so that the bronze is covered and becomes invisible to the eye. Will anyone say it has been damaged in its own essence because of the addition of the wax or of the other materials? Will he not say that both natures, the bronze and the wax or gold, are preserved in it unharmed? And then, can we not say that they have become four statues because of the addition? So by the same example, inferring great things from small ones and glimpsing the truth as in a mirror through faint images, you will understand that in Christ too there are two natures but one hypostasis, and you will never suspect that an addition has been made to the Trinity.

Of Anastasius of Antioch, from the work Against the Arbiter. Even if man is sometimes said to be of one nature, it is not the individual man that is meant but man in general, because the form is the same and the structure is alike; here “nature” is taken in place of the common form and of what is natural. Again, then, soul and body are not one nature: the soul is rational, intellectual and incorporeal, while the body is gross, mortal and irrational. And since they are set against each other as not being of one nature in essence, man is not, after all, of one essence. To put it another way: if every definition reveals the natures of the things it covers, and man is defined as a rational, mortal living being, and rational is not the same as mortal by the principle of nature, then man would not be of one nature according to the rule of his own definition. If man is ever said to be of one nature, the word “nature” is used in place of “form,” as when we say that man does not differ from man by any difference of nature, but that men are by nature alike to one another in the principle of their constitution, so that all are brought under one definition. And this is not strange, since we sometimes call all created and made things together, in general, whether rational or corporeal, of one nature, in respect of their very being as created, in contrast to the uncreated and unmade divine nature. Among all the other teachers, Athanasius, who is among the saints, shows this plainly in his work against those who blaspheme the Holy Spirit, where he says: “That the Spirit is above creation, other than the nature of created things and proper to the Godhead, can again be seen from this as well,” and so on. Therefore the individual and particular man would not be of one nature, but of one hypostasis and two natures.

Of Anastasius the presbyter, a discourse on God's formation of man “according to the image and according to the likeness.” I met one of the interpreters of Scripture, and he told me that once, while he was studying the holy Scripture, it suddenly happened that the eyes of his mind were opened, as it were, and he saw that the whole structure of creation and of everything in it portrays the image and pattern of the incarnation of God the Word. This is why Paul says of Christ that “all things were created through him and for him.” Those who mean to debate wisely and sensibly with the heretics about the properties of Christ, whether about will or about energy, must before any discussion require them to set out in writing the definitions listed below, for their folly is easily exposed by these. The holy Fathers spoke of two perfections in Christ, that is, that he is perfect in Godhead and likewise perfect in manhood. So we must require them to state in definitions, if they actually know: What is the definition of truly consubstantial? What is the definition of perfect and complete? What is the definition of a rational soul? What is the definition of an irrational [?] soul? And what is the definition of the soul of Christ? And what is a fleshly will? And what is soul [?]? And what is divine? And if they manage to define these terms in the manner of the Fathers and not of the Greeks, they fall, refuted by their own words. For just as the Word's consubstantiality with the Father shows him to be God lacking nothing, so in every respect the consubstantiality of his body and soul with us presents him as man lacking nothing. We urge our brothers in the Lord to discuss with the opponents the question of energies and wills with great reverence and circumspection,

and above all with those who cannot take it in, for “not all have faith,” as Paul says. And let us not, like some fools, shout recklessly, with a shameless face and the most brazen voice, “two natural wills” and “two natural energies” and “two natural this and that,” but let us speak with reverence, fear of God and circumspection. For it is possible to speak piously of the two natures in Christ. In the same way it is possible to speak of wills and energies in him either rightly or perversely. Diodore and Nestorius also speak of two natures of Christ, but wrongly [?]. And Theodore of Antioch and Arius of Alexandria speak of two wills, but opposed ones. Mani the Persian also speaks of two energies, one of a good God and another of an evil one. So I beg you: let us answer our opponents with all circumspection, telling them at once that if anyone says there is in Christ a fleshly or worldly will, or any energy at all opposed to his Godhead, or a will contrary [?] to God the Word, let him be condemned. For everything that the form of the servant possessed was subject to, and moved by, the nod and will of the form of the Master, God the Word. But so that we do not make his divine nature subject to passions, or the Word subordinate to the Father like a servant, we assign to each nature of Christ, without dividing them, what is proper to it.
