SERMON I. — FOUR DISCOURSES OF THE SAME ANASTASIUS [?]. On the Transfiguration of our Lord Jesus [Christ]. Jesus, who loves mankind, appeared to the world as a good teacher, since he is also God, and said to his disciples: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it; but whoever loses his soul for my sake will find it. For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world but forfeits his soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul? For the Son of Man is going to come in the glory of his Father with his holy angels, and then he will repay each according to his works.” “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself”: that is, every human way of thinking. And not only that, but also, like me, “Let him take up his cross and follow me.” We have learned from his own words that Paul did this. Not only was he crucified to the world and the world crucified to him; he also transformed life itself. He no longer lived himself, nor moved or acted on his own, but had Christ working in him as his very life. For he gave himself up

completely. He put his own will to death and laid himself wholly beneath the divine will, so that, if I may dare to coin a name, Paul should be called “Christ-living” [?] rather than living, for his life was Christ. This is how those who wish to belong to him must walk behind him and follow him. For there are two wills, which are generally opposed, the divine and the human; and since it is not possible to live without these, or without one of them [?], it is clear that whoever is fastened to the one has turned away from the other, and the reverse. So whoever wishes to walk behind the Lord will hate every human will, and, having exchanged the life he led before, let him follow in this way, leaving himself behind, as it were, and transforming all the powers of his soul. For whoever truly wishes to find his soul, as it wanders among the vanities of life and its dreamlike fantasies, must first lose it from the life it had in itself; and then he will find it with a good finding. But as long as he is attached to the matter of the world, he cannot recognize the loss he is in. Clearly, then, he will not seek the lost soul as he must, nor will he find it. For just as there are two lives and two deaths, one according to God and one according to the world, as Paul clearly shows [?] when he speaks of living to sin and to righteousness, so there are two losses of the soul: one blameworthy, the other praiseworthy. And just as whoever lives to sin is dead to righteousness, and conversely whoever lives to righteousness is dead to sin, so whoever follows the wills of the flesh walks behind the flesh, and has lost the walk behind the Lord. But whoever has hated the life of the flesh [?], or rather its loss [?], and says in effect, “I will walk behind my God,” has exchanged the blameworthy loss and gained the praiseworthy one. For to be lost to the world is to be found by God, and to be found by the world is to be lost to God. And what a foolish plan it is to find the whole world, or gain some of it, and hold it as one's own possession, but to forfeit and lose one's soul! For what can be given in exchange for a soul? Or what ransom will anyone pay for it? Nothing material is of equal value to it. Only the soul itself can be given in exchange for itself, and nothing else at all. For the Son, receiving the authority to judge from the Father, is going to come to repay each according to his works. Then nothing that surrounds us can help us. We shall all stand naked before the judgment seat, stripped of what belongs to others (and everything that surrounds us belongs to others), and books will be opened to convict us. Through what has been imprinted on the conscience, they will show whom each of us followed more, the flesh or the Spirit, Christ or the world, and which loss of the soul each chose, the loss from God or the loss from the world. And when this fearful and most exact inquiry takes place, the one who received authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man, will give to each his due portion.

For he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels, his ministering spirits. He will no longer be without form or beauty, as he appeared to the world now, but "fairer in beauty than the sons of men." He has changed his own body into incorruption and shows that what was changed in its elements through the resurrection has become spiritual and heavenly. We too have this as a pledge that our own elements will be changed and our bodies transformed. And so that we may hold the unseen part of this hope securely, he wishes even now to show the chosen among the disciples the change that will take place then. "In a moment," says Paul, "in the twinkling of an eye." That is why he says, "Truly I tell you, there are some of those standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom." How this came about we shall learn from what follows. "And it came to pass after six days that Jesus took Peter and James and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain by themselves, and Jesus was transfigured before them. His face shone like the sun, and his clothes became white as snow. And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them, talking with him." We must not hear these things in a merely literal way, or think that the narrative goes no further than the words, showing only what the words themselves show. Rather, it is a distinct mystagogy [?], and a foretaste of the enjoyment of the good things that will be ours after this life — or rather the saints', not ours. That is why after six days he fulfils the promise he had made to the disciples. The promise was this: "There are some of those standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God," which is to be revealed after the end of this grosser world. Therefore after six days he took those who had to learn the more divine mysteries of the kingdom before they tasted death. After the six comes the seventh, the holy rest, on which no work may be done. For in six days God made heaven and earth, and on the seventh he rested and sanctified it. So the promise was made on the first day, and the fulfilment of the promise again on the first. The number six, then, corresponds to this grosser world, which is made up of its own days and completed by them. It is a symbol of generation, since it contains in itself the male and the female, whose union brings about bodily generation. After their generation comes next the seventh, in which they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God in [Editorial notes:] Αὐτῷ μόνῳ: read αὐτὸ μόνον. Ἡ πρώτη: perhaps τῇ πρώτῃ.

heaven. That is why the number seven is also called virgin. Likewise the seventh day is holy: it brings every work of service to rest and makes all settle, each in his own place. After this, then, he takes the three chosen disciples. It was not fitting for Judas to witness such great mysteries. But neither was it right for him alone to be left out of the vision, in case the apparent preference for the others gave him a pretext for betrayal. So Jesus takes only the three and leads them up a high mountain (and what is higher than his glory?), and by themselves, for the immaterial life is solitary. He led them up from below, not so much in place as in contemplation; that is, he made them able to receive his surpassing radiance. Then he was transfigured before them. Long ago Jesus the Saviour was also transformed, not before men but before his own Father, when he, "being in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant." At that time he veiled the divine form by being transformed into the form of a servant. Now he restores the form of the servant to his natural form. He does not put off the servile substance, but makes it radiant with the divine properties. So he was transfigured before them, showing them that in this way he will one day refashion the body of our lowliness, making it conformed to the body of his glory. "And his face shone," it says, "like the sun, and his clothes became white as snow." This is not written in order to compare him to the sun or to snow (for how can the incomparable be compared?). But nothing material is brighter than the sun or whiter than snow. So, wishing to convey in a measured way how far the light and the brightness surpassed all else, the evangelist made the comparison through things familiar to us. The radiance of his clothes shows the change of our bodies, for we have become his garment, since he clothed himself with our flesh. Perhaps, too, his face shining like the sun is a symbolic hint at his own body, while his clothes white as snow hint at those who are cleansed through him by his transforming and changing power. That is why the garment, understood in this way, is likened to snow: snow too is water that has been transformed and turned to vapour. That our nature became his clothing, and will again, let us hear from Isaiah, to whom God speaks of him: "As I live, says the Lord, you shall clothe yourself with them all, and put them on like a bride's adornment." He was transfigured, then, and his face shone like the sun, and his clothes became white as snow; and Moses and Elijah appeared to them, talking with him. Having become more clear-sighted,

Sermon I. — On the Transfiguration. the apostles, since they had been lifted up with Jesus on the mountain, barely recognized that Moses and Elijah were then talking with Jesus, having been transfigured together with him. For unless they had been transfigured with him, they would not have been talking with him. According to Luke, they were speaking with Jesus about his departure, which he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem. And from them the disciples heard about the things they had failed to understand when Jesus once told them. That was when Peter, setting his mind on human things, rebuked Jesus for saying that he would be killed by men and raised from the dead on the third day. So, as I said, Moses and Elijah speak in harmony with Jesus; that is, the Law and the Prophets. When their words are transfigured and the shadows of the Law are removed, then Moses too will be believed, the faithful servant who wrote everything about Christ. From his own words he will clearly set forth the departure that Christ was to accomplish in Jerusalem. Some ask where, or how, or by what signs the disciples recognized the prophets. This does not seem to me a clever question or one worth investigating. They had risen to such a height that they were deemed worthy of such a vision, which the one who revealed himself to them, transfigured together with the prophets, called the kingdom of heaven. How then could they fail to recognize their fellow initiates? The apostles too were certainly prophets, and prophets meeting with prophets share one and the same [?], especially when Jesus is present, enlightening the ruling faculty and shaping the mind toward his own divine form. "And Peter answered and said to Jesus, 'Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you wish, let us make three tents here, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.'" Peter perceived how intelligible things differ from sensible ones, and he chooses the better over the worse. Yet he did not yet fully understand what he had seen; otherwise he would not have concerned himself with tents among intelligible things. Perhaps he was also still anxious for his teacher because of the death Jesus had foretold, which the figures who appeared were also discussing with Jesus. For they agreed in saying that this departure would take place in Jerusalem. Perhaps for this reason he asked the teacher to stay there instead, and by no means to give himself up to the Pharisees and scribes who envied him. For he probably thought that none of those plotting against him would come to him on the mountain,
and that what was to happen in Jerusalem could not happen otherwise, or in another place [?]. "It is good, then,
for us to be with Moses and Elijah," rather than to go away to the unholy, God-killing priests. And if

you consider what is said: "Let us make here," he says, [?] "three tents, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah." In apparently trying to spare his teacher, he did not realize that he was becoming a hindrance to the salvation of the world, as

Luke remarks when he says, "not knowing what he was saying." And Mark says, "For he did not know what he had said, or what it meant." Those who went up with Jesus should stand higher in place [?]. "While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them, and a voice from the cloud said, 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.' When the disciples heard this, they fell on their faces and were greatly afraid. And Jesus came and touched them, saying, 'Rise, and do not be afraid.' And when they lifted up their eyes, they saw no one but Jesus alone." While Peter was still speaking these words of attachment to his teacher, a bright cloud from above overshadowed them. And a voice came from the cloud correcting Peter, and perhaps also his fellow disciples, who wanted the same as he did and were saying they should stay on the mountain. The correction was that they should think nothing contrary to the beloved Son, but listen to him and follow his will, for it brings salvation to all people. What we should understand by this cloud must be sought from similar passages in Scripture. We find that Moses too entered the cloud when it covered the mountain in the desert of Horeb, and he is said to have entered the thick darkness where God was. Again, of old the cloud covered the tent of witness in various ways, and from there God was heard speaking to Moses. A pillar of cloud also went before the people, giving dew by day but blazing with fire by night. Isaiah too foretells that the Lord will come into Egypt on a light cloud. We also hear about Solomon that when he built and consecrated the temple, the cloud filled the house, and the priests could not enter and minister because of the cloud. These passages, and more like them, can be gathered from the whole of Scripture to explain and clarify the meaning before us. They help us know what the cloud was that overshadowed all who appeared, together with the onlookers, and from which the voice was heard saying, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him." We must regard the clouds mentioned as akin to one another; or rather, we should not hesitate to say that they are all one. We must not suppose it to be an exhalation from the earth, or water turned to vapour, or a condensation of air, or anything airy at all belonging to bodily substance. It is the knowledge of the divine nature that we can attain and that reaches us, which is more fittingly called "majesty," as David names it. For since those subject to generation and corruption cannot grasp the divine essence, through the ways that are possible

he appears to us, and in those after him who are near him [?]; that is why he has also spoken to us through prophets. When we hear a man saying, "I am the Lord your God," we do not believe that the man, Isaiah for instance, is God, but that God is the one who speaks in him. So even if the voice belonged to the cloud, from which it was heard, it was clearly first and foremost the voice of the Father. He bore witness to Christ's sonship, thundering through a rational nature that drew near to him. There are also lesser clouds, which give voice and serve as interpreters of the word, as in "The clouds gave forth a voice." They are also commanded not to rain on the thorn-bearing vineyard, the bodily house of Israel. I say that these are the prophets, who rain down the word and water those who need to drink. But this cloud rises above all of them and overshadows all; that is, it takes thought for all. "This," then, it says, "is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him." It does not say "the loved Son," but rather "the beloved" [that is, the lovable]. For what is loved is not necessarily lovable, but what is lovable is also loved. What is lovable is wholly so by nature, whereas what is loved is not necessarily so by nature, but by good pleasure. The Son, then, being one, is both: lovable, and, if I may put it this way, "well-pleasing." For he took on something of a different essence from himself, and joined [?] what was not consubstantial with him to show forth one hypostasis. So in his testimony the Father showed us the difference. He did not separate what had been united (for how can what God has joined be separated?). Rather, he showed the union of things of different natures, and the one Son made up of them, Christ the Lord, one beloved Son. It was the Father's good pleasure that all creation should worship this Son and listen to him. When the apostles were found worthy of this majestic voice, they fell on their faces, submitting to the voice that came from above, and were greatly afraid. Perhaps this was because of their earlier disobedience: they learned that they had been thinking contrary to the Father's good pleasure by recoiling from the death of the Son, through which salvation had been stored up beforehand for all people, according to the Father's ancient counsel. While they were terrified and lying on the ground, "Jesus came near and touched them, saying, 'Rise, and do not be afraid.'" For no one could drive away [?] that fear and dread [?] except the Son alone, who always bids those who come near him to take courage. Variant readings and notes. Ἀκούοντος: read ἀκούοντες. [On the phrase] "thundering through a rational nature that drew near to him."

Persuaded, they lifted up their eyes, which had perhaps been dimmed by fear, and when they lifted them they saw Jesus alone. Up to this point the veiled showing of the kingdom of heaven took place. "And as they were coming down from the mountain, Jesus commanded them, saying, 'Tell no one the vision until the Son of Man has risen.'" Why, then, did he forbid them to recount what they had seen, and to reveal to anyone the mystery of the resurrection? Because the Firstborn from the dead had to rise first, confirming the resurrection by deed; only then would the common resurrection of all be made known through testimony. For who would have believed what they said, when even the chosen among the apostles did not believe? Peter even regarded what was said about the Saviour's death as blasphemous, until the

Today, my excellent children, bringing a discourse [?] before you, I trust that I shall gladden the Church with this account. Today, as I reveal to us the joining and binding together of God the Word with our flesh, [I ...] you, rejoicing, from here

into the foundations of Zion, he who binds together things whose nature cannot be bound, and makes one what are foreign to each other in essence. Let us rejoice, then, as is fitting, with her who received the grace, and with Gabriel let us greet the Mother of our God, saying, "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you." For you have become for us the way of salvation, the ascent to heaven, the place of rest, and the tent of refreshment in which the Lord made his dwelling. That is why, with all generations, we call you blessed, you alone among women. The sun did not scorch you by bringing the flame of pleasure, nor did the flowing power of the moon harm you by night. For you did not let the foot of your soul be moved, but remained unswerving, having planted it firmly on the rock. And the Lord kept you: he alone entered into you and went forth from you, and he kept you shut and sealed for ever. Hail, then, O Mother and Virgin, food of life and fountain of immortality! For from you came forth the destroyer of corruption, the one who put death to death. So, brethren, having said these things to the Mother of God as best we can, let us now turn to ourselves. Let us recognize the power of this day, and today let us renew our birth. This day is for us a holy convocation, on which we were fashioned and returned to the ancient life. What I say may perhaps seem strange to you. Yet it will be said, since God gives the power and supplies speech to the speaker. But where should we begin the account, if not from the words of the evangelist? Let him begin the discourse for us, since he also made this day known. "In the sixth month," he says, "the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man named Joseph, of the house and family of David; and the virgin's name was Mary." And perhaps someone who examines such matters closely might ask: What is the sixth month, and from where is it counted? To make the point clear to him, let us go back to what comes a little earlier in the Gospel: "and she hid herself for five months," and so on. Then it adds: "In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent to Mary." But he might reply that even so the [?] remains. For when the evangelist says, "After these days Elizabeth conceived," he did not indicate which days. It seems to me that whoever says this raises a fair question. But he will learn if he lends his ear to listen and takes in what is said with understanding. Once a year the priest, according to the law, enters [Footnotes:] Ezek. 44:2. Luke 1:25, 27. Luke 1:24.

the Holy of Holies, making atonement for the people. That is why they call this feast "Atonement," or "the Day of Atonement," and "the day of humiliation," and "the great fast." It is held on the tenth day of the seventh month, which is October, called Tishri by the Hebrews; for the Hebrews begin the year in April. On the tenth day of the seventh lunar month, then, Zechariah was serving as priest. He saw the angelic vision and received the good news of the Baptist's birth. After this, when he had completed his course of service, he went back to his house. That course ends when the moon has become full, at what is called the full moon. Then his wife Elizabeth conceived, and she hid herself for the five months, perhaps blushing because of the grey hair blossoming on her, that such a

angel says to the Virgin: "And behold, your kinswoman too has conceived a son in her old age, and this is the sixth month for her who was called barren." This led us to a bigger question, and one of the more zealous raised an objection. "If he says," the objector argued, "that the greeting, that is, the Annunciation, took place at some point in the course of the month, why is it celebrated today, that is, on the twenty-fifth, and not on some other day of the month?" It would be very easy to answer him: "You would have raised the same difficulty about any other day." Yet let us offer a defence, since the follow-up question does not seem unreasonable. We speak without claiming that this is the truth, and without holding to our own account alone. We are freely sharing with you what has occurred to us, and training you to seek a truer solution than this one. When you find it, let this one remain [?] and not be thought worthy of being written down at all. This world was brought into being and is measured by time, so it certainly began from some motion. And what could that be but a temporal beginning? For we have not been taught to call the world eternal, nor have the Churches of God. Nothing is eternal whose parts are subject to corruption and change; whenever the parts of a thing perish, the whole is certainly capable of corruption too. If the parts of the world perish, then clearly the whole will perish as well. Therefore it is not eternal. And if it is not eternal, it had a beginning of its being and a beginning of its generation, which [?]

[…] world, as has been shown. Surely it was fitting that the wisdom of God, which created and fashioned all things in order and justice, should begin creation [?] here and give time its beginning, since time itself entered together with created things. It was fitting to begin straight away from equality: from justice [?] in the things that are distinguished and divided, and from perfectly equal shares. The beginning of spring received this equality from the very first, at creation, and keeps it to this day. It mediates between cold and heat and escapes the harm that each brings by its excess. Then it grants more to the light and to the length of the day, and carries off darkness as plunder for the rule of light. For light had to be judged more honourable than darkness, had to be. Darkness has no substance of its own; light came into being at God's first word, though it had not existed before, and it was declared to be good. From this the Hebrews also call this month the first. They probably did so from of old and from their fathers, and it was also laid down for them by law through Moses: "This month," he says, "shall be the first for you among the months of the year." Elsewhere Moses calls it the month of new things, because it is a memorial of the beginning of the new creation and of the things made in the beginning. He had also received from the fathers the knowledge that this month is the beginning of time. In the account of the flood we clearly find the month after Nisan called the second. For this is the Hebrews' name for the first month, which the Romans call April and the Macedonians Xanthicus. Nisan means "flowering," for among the Hebrews nissa means a flower. Perhaps Xanthicus too is really Anthicus and got the name Xanthicus by an added letter. Whether Anthicus or Xanthicus, it takes its name from the blossoming in the air. So the first month is the one that begins at the spring equinox. It is first by nature, as the beginning of time, created together with the bringing forth of all that exists. The equinox, when no part of the preceding time remains in the sun's course, falls on the twenty-[fifth] of March, that is, the month of Dystrus. It still coincides with that day even now, when the four-year cycle of the so-called bissextile year completes the motion into a whole day. In the other three years, because of the leftover quarter, it falls no longer on the twenty-[fifth], [but on the] [Notes: "Demeg[orias]": read "demiourgias" (creation). "Of justice": perhaps "of the season." "[…] entered with created things" [?]]

twenty-]first. For this reason the equinox falls irregularly. Next spring begins, which at once transforms everything and moves it toward beauty and birth. If this is so, we take the twentieth of March to be the beginning of the visible world. For what was being brought into being certainly had to come into being in the most beautiful of the seasons. The most beautiful season is spring, as our senses themselves testify. We see everything moving toward multiplication and growth at that time, out of reverence for the first command: "Increase and multiply." Spring, then, is the most beautiful season, and it begins from the equinox, the day on which God began the works that came into being. He fashioned man on the sixth day, so we have fixed the making of man on the [twenty-fifth] of March, for the twenty-fifth is the sixth day from the twentieth. This being so, what day should the one who fashioned man in the beginning have appointed for himself to be joined with flesh? For our salvation he willingly made himself subject to flesh and birth and our sufferings, so as to free us who were held captive by sin. So it was fitting that he should begin to be formed on the same day on which we too began to come into being. For he was called the second Adam, since he took on everything that belonged to the first except sin alone. If he took on everything, why would he have overlooked this, the time truly worthy of his wise plan for us? The sinner had to be refashioned at the time when he was fashioned. Therefore on that day "Gabriel was sent" to announce to the Virgin the birth without corruption and to proclaim to her in advance the salvation that would come through her to the nations. With the greeting, "the Word became flesh," refashioning the creature that sin had corrupted when it entered along with the words of the evil serpent. The flesh corrupted by the hissing of the serpent had to return to incorruption through the greeting of the angel, had to. Just as death was brought about through a woman, so salvation had to be accomplished through a woman. Because of the first woman, who was stolen away by pleasure, we all died; [through this woman we were made alive.] We received not only what we had fallen from, but far greater and richer things, which the human mind cannot picture, the eye cannot reach, and the ear is too weak to take in. This is the feast and festival we keep. It is the Annunciation of this holy and revered Virgin and the birthday of the whole world, because all things were transformed into order, and the former disorder

received order. For our sake the one who fashioned us became like us. He renewed his image, which had grown old and been corrupted, and reshaped it into an abundance of beauty, all but crying out to us: "Since on this day you were fashioned and then fell away and were dragged down to death, on this day I, the Fashioner, am fashioned for your sake. By this flesh of mine, now being fashioned, I will lead you back to your former life. That is why I grapple with death and put it to death, as was only right." To confirm what we have said from the Fathers, and to add a kind of ornament that will give it charm, hear what Gregory, who received the title of Theologian, says about the spring turning of the year. Urging us toward New Sunday in the oration entitled [?], he says: "Let the heaven be new for you, and the earth new, as you grasp both these things and their meaning. See what the visible world is like. The queen of seasons escorts the queen of days in procession and brings as gifts everything most beautiful and delightful." He strings together many praises of the spring season, and so shows that he took it to be the prelude and the beginning, and whatever else one might call it, the release [?] and the fixing of time, compared with the season before it. But in my love for the subject I am overrunning the time, and the sun has already gone down toward its setting. Should I not end my discourse here, so that I do not [weary?] you by saying too much about these things and become tiresome to you? Let us therefore sing the praises of him who became flesh for our sake, and through him and with him send up glory and honour to the Father and the Holy Spirit. For to him belong praise and greatness and majesty, now and always, to the ages of ages. Amen.

What does the great Gabriel want with us on earth again? Has he [come down?] to us once more? What hidden mysteries of God is he serving? The angel does not carry out commands about small matters, but about truly awe-inspiring ones. The things entrusted to him are great. What is revealed through him could easily be grasped by no one else. He alone is entrusted with the ineffable treasures of God's wisdom, and is given light into the depth of his unsearchable judgments. He came to us once to give understanding to Daniel, the man of desires. He came to teach him the succession of kings and the end of the world, to reveal the resurrection, to foretell the judgment rendered to each according to its order, and to make plain the revelation of the years to come. He came again to announce to his father the wondrous birth of the divine Baptist, and to point to the joining of human beings with God through him. For even if

now, entrusted with this, he came to those written of [?]. You who are worthy to believe what is written, consider this: barren women bear children; old men become fathers; babies leap in the womb; a priest is condemned [?] to silence for his unbelief […]

Each of the holy angels is entrusted with something different, but he alone is entrusted with the chief point of all: God conceived without seed in a virgin's womb, the Holy Spirit working together for the birth, and the Father and God over all bidding him say to the Virgin: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you." O generous and divine word! O boundless love for mankind and goodness! O truly angelic ministry! O blessed Virgin, deemed worthy of such words, or rather, deemed worthy to serve [?] such things! You conceived without union; you gave birth without marriage; you alone became Mother and Virgin at once. For the birth did not break your virginity, and the conception did not destroy your incorruption. The treasure of your virginity remains [?] inviolate even after the birth. You nursed with milk, as an infant, the one who gives food to all flesh. You drew to your breast, as a baby, the one who makes milk flow for mothers to nourish the babies they bear. For you became the mother not of a mere man, nor of some prophet, nor of one in whom God dwells, but the true mother of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ. Who will tell of the mighty acts of the Lord? What ear will be able to take them in? What words will be found worthy to express what the mind grasps? Until you, women heard: "In sorrow you shall bear children." That divine command ran against all of them like a decree of inheritance [?], and remained indissoluble and unchangeable. From now on, through you, the female sex will hear: "Rejoice, women," for they have received as the beginning of their rejoicing the only one among virgins who is full of grace: the fair, the spotless, the holy Mary, Mother of God. Such is the good news the great angel brings to the Virgin, and with his words the only-begotten Son of God entered the virgin's womb. A womb contained him whom heaven could not contain at all. He who is above us became an embryo for our sake, growing little by little and coming to bodily completion: the all-perfect Word of God, who upholds all things by the word of his power. The Maker of the ages takes a beginning in time, he who exists before the ages. The Creator of human beings became a human being and gained a mother from among us. The only Son of God by nature took flesh from her, of one substance with ours. But speech does not rise as high as these marvels, and no mortal tongue can worthily proclaim the great

works of God. So come, Isaiah, most powerful and most eloquent of the prophets. Come, [?] teach us the great things of God. Sing through the Spirit of what has come to pass. Foretell it, so that what is announced may be heard. Glorify the one who enlightens whom he wills. Make the incredible believable [?] by your prophecy. "Behold," he says, "the Virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel." Speak again, prophet, the hymn of praise for these things: "O Lord God, I will glorify you, I will sing praise to your name, for you have done wonderful things, an ancient and true counsel. So be it, Lord." And what was God's ancient and true counsel? That all of us should be saved. He gave us being, so surely he would give us well-being even more. He would call his own creature back to its ancient dwelling and to keeping the commandment. Through that commandment the promise of life in us was without end, and we rightly lost it by not keeping the commandment. But you, O divine and blessed Virgin, ladder stretched up to heaven, gate of paradise, [guide?] to incorruption, union and bond of human beings with God, seal our discourse for us: in Christ Jesus our Lord, through whom and with whom be glory and might to the Father, with the all-holy and life-giving Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.
By Anastasius, Patriarch of Theoupolis, Great Antioch [?], on the three holy Lents: where we received the custom of keeping them, and that those who transgress them [break the law?] […]

We follow the apostolic traditions and ordinances and the written laws of our holy Fathers. So we ought not to need inquiries, or to invent empty and futile pretexts for setting aside what they defined. We ought instead to hold carefully to what they defined, both in their divine canons and in the holy writings of theirs that survive, and in the holy sayings handed down by their tradition, and to regard and revere these as words of God. But the devil hates what is good and deceives. Long ago he corrupted the commandment of fasting given to the first-formed man in paradise, led him on to eat from the tree, and handed him over to death. He does not stop slandering, to this day, the holy commands [Note (1): "Of Anastasius, on the three Lents."]

given by God and by his saints for the salvation of our race. Just now he has crept in especially among some of our own people. They are not only lay people, or the ignorant and illiterate, but even those who pride themselves on their learning and raise their eyebrows over their great wisdom. I mean bishops, metropolitans, priests, deacons and the rest of the clergy, and even, I suppose, the monks themselves, "whose god is their belly." They teach quite shamelessly and impudently that only one fast was handed down by the holy apostles and the divine Fathers: the one called the Great Fast. The fast of the Nativity of Christ, which some also call the fast of St Philip (for a reason we will give further on), and the fast before the commemoration of the holy chief apostles Peter and Paul, they say did not come from any ordinance of the apostles or the Fathers. They call them inventions and personal preferences of certain monks who keep these two fasts. So some of those who resist God's ordinance abstain for eighteen days only from meat, cheese and eggs. Some abstain only from meat and eat everything else, except on one day. Others likewise abstain for only twelve days, others six, and others four. And they are not content to go astray themselves alone; they also drag along crowds of simple folk, so that the sin will not be theirs alone. But they will surely suffer a greater punishment, because they cause many to stumble and lead them away from the straight path. For if whoever [causes] one [Note (2): "Of the Nativity of Christ" [?] […] fast […] in Reg. 912 (now 3026), which also reads: "Count from after Meatfare, that is, from the Monday of the first week [?], until the Christian Pascha [?]. As many days as are found from the Monday of Renewal Week until the third of May, expect that many in the summer as well […]"]

setting them aside and telling lies against them, out of conceit and arrogance and their inner [?] love of pleasure and gluttony. They do not even tremble at the Lord's verdict: "Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it would be better for him [that a] millstone […]," and the rest, which everyone knows. So let them hear the apostolic and patristic traditions mentioned above about these fasts. "And the Lord said to Moses: Speak to the sons of Israel and say: Keep three seasons of the year for me. or on Wednesday or Friday, let him be deposed, unless he is prevented by illness." About the Lent of the Nativity of Christ, it is written in the Travels of St Philip that he went about preaching the word of truth and came, teaching, to Hierapolis in Asia, together with Bartholomew and his sister Mariamne. That city worshipped the viper. They seized the apostles and put them through many tortures, since they would not accept them at all and could not bear even to hear the divine word. The one exception was the man who first received the apostles: he was baptized with his whole household and family, and so was the proconsul's wife. They led Philip out, pierced his ankles and crucified him head downward. They hung Bartholomew on a tree near him, and they held Mariamne in prison. When St John came there, Philip told him that they should ask for fire to come down from heaven and consume them all, but the apostle John prevented this. After John had left and three days had passed, St Philip prayed. The earth opened its mouth and brought all the idolaters down alive into Hades. After this the Saviour appeared to him and reminded him of his commandment not to repay evil for evil, and the rest. Then he added: "Since you disobeyed my commandment and harmed those who grieved you, you will fall asleep here and be carried in glory by my holy angels as far as paradise. But you will not enter. You will stand outside for forty days, grieving and kept back by the flaming sword, because you grieved those who wr[onged you] [Note (11): "Seizing the apostles": […] joining it with "system" [?] […]]

onged you. Then you will enter and receive the place prepared for you." He brought back up those who had been brought down into Hades, and ascended into heaven. Then Philip charged Bartholomew and Mariamne to tell James and the other apostles to fast and pray for him for forty days. So the apostles appointed a fast and prayer of forty days for all the faithful. It was kept by the holy Fathers and by the seven ecumenical councils. The fast laid down was not one of five or eight or ten days, but of forty. It is called "of the Nativity of Christ" because the saving birth of our Lord Jesus Christ came at the end of the forty days. So two good things result. We fulfil the tradition of the apostles, and we are purified in advance to meet and worship our Lord Jesus Christ, who was born without defilement and ineffably of the holy Theotokos and Ever-Virgin. The fast after Pentecost is the one mentioned in the Constitutions of the holy apostles. In them they say: "After Pentecost keep festival for one week, and after that, fast. For it is right to rejoice at the gift of God, and after the relaxation to fast. For Moses and Elijah fasted forty days, and for three weeks Daniel ate no pleasant bread, and neither meat nor wine entered his mouth." This fast was therefore kept until the Dormition of the Theotokos. But the holy Fathers cut it short as a pastoral concession. One reason was that it coincided with the fasts of other peoples, such as the Armenians, Jacobites and Nestorians, and often the Ishmaelites as well. Another reason, as it seems to me, was people's negligence and lack of zeal. So it was laid down that we fast until the feast of the holy apostles and then break the fast. Then we fast from the beginning of August until the Dormition of the Theotokos and break the fast again. In this we have the exhortation of the Apostolic Constitutions.

Catechist: What is your religion, sir?
Catechumen: I am a Christian.
And what is a Christian?
One who lives according to God, and conducts his life piously, in a way pleasing to God, and uprightly.
In theology, how many natures do you confess?
One.
Which is it?
The Godhead.
What is God?
An uncaused being, the cause of all things that exist; that is, all-powerful, almighty, the cause beyond being of every cause and nature. [?] in one [?] Father; and in one Son and God, begotten of God the Father; and in one Holy Spirit, God, proceeding from [?].
In what does the Son differ from the Father?
In hypostasis: in that the Father is unbegotten, while the Son is begotten, for he is from the Father.
In what does the Holy Spirit differ from the Father and the Son?
In hypostasis, in that he proceeds.
So then, do you believe in three gods?

But in three natures? [?] And yet you have counted three gods; how then do you say, "God forbid"? I did not count three [?]; rather, I speak of the three because of the threefold hypostatic being of the consubstantial and undivided [?] Trinity. For since the Father is one God, and the Son is one God, and the Holy Spirit is one God, and one

Godhead is defined in three hypostases, and one essence, and kingship, and power, and nature.
And what is essence?
A self-subsistent thing, needing nothing else for its own existence.
What is nature?
The universal thing that encompasses the hypostases under it. Or thus: the true existence of things; so that essence, nature and form are one and the same thing.
How many hypostases do you confess in the Godhead?
Three: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
What is a hypostasis?
An essence with certain properties, differing in number from others of the same species; that is, a consubstantial person. And when speaking of God we say the persons are incorporeal and without shape.
What is proper to each of the three hypostases, and what is common?
Proper to the Father is being unbegotten, to the Son being begotten, and to the Holy Spirit proceeding; common are the Godhead and the kingship.
How many natures do you confess in the economy?
Two, Godhead and humanity, so that the same Son is perfect God and perfect man.
How many natural wills and operations do you confess in Christ?
Two: one divine and one human.
What is the divine will?
To cleanse lepers, as in, "I will; be cleansed," and things like this; and, "Go; as you have believed, let it be done for you."
What is the divine operation?
That all people be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth; as in, "My Father is working until now, and I am working."
What is the human will?
To ask to drink, which happened also on the cross, and to ask to eat, as in, "Have you anything to eat?"

What is the human operation?
Walking, growing weary, and the like.
How many hypostases do you confess in the confession concerning the Son?
One, so that the same one is the one Son of God and the Son of the Virgin.
In what does the Son share with the Father and the Holy Spirit?
He shares with them in the nature of his Godhead, inasmuch as he is perfect God; and he shares with human beings in the nature of his humanity, inasmuch as he is also perfect man.

What is God? If you wish to know what God is and how he is worshipped, listen attentively and learn the truth. The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit have one will, one wisdom, one power. It is not that one exists before the ages and another after the ages; rather, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit exist together, the Son in the Father and the Spirit in the Son, for their nature is joined. Hence there is one nature and one Godhead: divided into three by reason of the hypostases, but arriving at unity by reason of the essence. For this reason, when we name the Father and confess the Son and the Holy Spirit, we speak of one God. The name "God" is common to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit; but "Father," "Son" and "Holy Spirit" are not common names, but belong to each hypostasis individually. For the Father is not called Son, and the Son is not called Father; and the Holy Spirit is called neither Father nor Son. But the Trinity is always named God. So when we speak of three hypostases, that is, three persons, we do not speak of three essences, or three natures, or three gods; rather, we confess one God, one essence or nature, so that we may not fall into Arianism. And when we speak of one essence or nature, we do not speak of one hypostasis, so that we may not fall into Sabellianism. Rather, we believe in three hypostases, that is, three persons, in one Godhead, one essence and nature. God is an essence beyond contemplation, an incomprehensible mind, a beauty beyond reach, an invisible greatness, a glory beyond conception. But when the truth had come, they did not think it good to live according to the figures and still follow them.
